items.title: F1 2026 Las Vegas GP starting grid after five penalties
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
The starting grid for Formula 1's 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix is a very different picture from the qualifying result thanks to multiple grid penalties.

Kimi Antonelli topped qualifying, but he won't start from pole position because he has a five-place grid penalty for taking the new Mercedes ADUO turbocharger this weekend.

He'll start from sixth place instead.

Oscar Piastri qualified seventh, but he'll start 17th because he took the new ADUO turbocharger (his penalty is twice that of Antonelli's because it's his first turbocharger breach, while Antonelli's is his second).

Carlos Sainz will move back six of his 10 places from 14th to 20th while Lance Stroll will go from 20th to 21st for a 10-place grid penalty. Ollie Bearman will remain 22nd and last after his 35-place engine penalty.

items.title: Plastic bag and a 'horrendous' weakness hurt Norris in Vegas
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
Lando Norris called McLaren's straightline speed "shocking" and "horrendous" after missing out on pole position for Formula 1's 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Norris was fourth fastest in Q3 and will start the race third on the grid thanks to a grid penalty for new world champion and pole winner Kimi Antonelli, but was frustrated to be 0.351 seconds off the pace.

"We're just shocking in the straights," Norris said. "Like, horrendous in the straight. 

"My lap was very good and it was easily my best lap. But to Kimi, we're eight tenths off in the last sector. 

"He has a perfect tow and he does a very good job. But comparing to most other people, we're too far off. 

"I have to start my lap 1.5 seconds off the car ahead, which means in every corner I'm losing at least a half a tenth to a tenth because of how much downforce I'm losing. 

"There's obviously a bigger gain at the end of the day in having a good slipstream, but we're having to make up for a pretty terrible loss of straightline speed and therefore we have to harm our cornering speed. 

"So we just haven't got the right balance, all in all, in terms of downforce, drag. It's made our life impossible to fight for our pole."

Team principal Andrea Stella also offered an unusual extra mitigating factor on Norris's side.

"I would like to mention that especially on Lando's side he has been quite unlucky, because the plastic bag got stuck in the floor and we lost quite a lot of downforce there," Stella explained.

"So, considering that one tenth of a second would have made a big difference, certainly there was one tenth of a second on a plastic bag, which is a bit of a shame."

Team-mate Oscar Piastri was over a second off the pace down in seventh, beaten by the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad in Q3.

And even though Norris described McLaren's deficit on the straights as something that's "been an issue all year", Piastri felt McLaren had been "caught a bit by surprise" by how much it was losing out in Vegas. 

"I don't think we expected it to be such a big problem," he said. "At Monza we were OK, and the strange part for us is it's mostly compared to the other Mercedes-powered cars. 

"So, maybe a lot of people took downforce off, and we didn't take enough off. But it seems like a pretty massive step that we were missing."

Stella said McLaren had "some concerns in terms of how suitable the demand of this circuit would be for our car" because of the team's shorter gear ratios and its known weakness in generating the same straightline performance as power unit supplier Mercedes.

"Certainly we have seen here trends that are similar to Monza and Baku, and in all conditions we were not particularly competitive," Stella summarised.

'Messy' or well executed?

Piastri called Q3 a "messy" session for McLaren, which left "a few things that we probably will review and see if we can do a slightly better job". 

"Even opening the lap here, there's a bit of a difference between cars, how much energy they use to Turn 1, and if that's half a second, that can be the difference of three or four tenths down the straight later in the lap," Piastri added. 

"So it's difficult to get right, but I think also my laps were a little bit messy as well."

As Antonelli's pole lap showed, all of this was massively overwhelmed by the towing effect - which was worth a significant chunk of extra laptime if executed correctly.

"I think Ferrari is the perfect example," Piastri said. "They didn't get a slipstream, or not a big enough slipstream, and they're out in Q2. 

"I think honestly, any of the top four teams could have done the same thing if they didn't get a tow. 

"So, it's a massive part of these kind of tracks in these cars, and you kind of just have to make do because maybe you can gain a tenth or two with the perfect [tyre] warm-up, but you look at Kimi, he's one second faster than me in the last sector. 

"No matter what you gain on the tyres, you're always going to lose it and a lot more on the tow."

Stella felt McLaren had executed that part well.

"What we have done better here is to mitigate this [weakness] from having really good positioning in qualifying," Stella said.

"The car was pretty much where we wanted it to be in qualifying, and this definitely helped, because I have to say that it seems like with these regulations, the drag reduction when you follow one car or even multiple cars is more than in the past, and therefore there is an even higher incentive to be positioned in the right place.

"I think this worked well in qualifying."

items.title: Super Formula Suzuka: Ohta takes title in dramatic fashion as Iwasa wins opener
Winners and losers from F1 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix qualifying
items.author: Jack Benyon
items.content:
The rain-affected Formula 1 practice sessions meant there was added emphasis on hitting the ground running in FP3 and carrying that through into Las Vegas Grand Prix qualifying.

Who nailed it when it mattered most, and who failed to deliver on their earlier promise?

Here's our pick of winners and losers:

Loser: Ferrari (11th and 12th)

It's been a rollercoaster year for Ferrari, but a double-Q2 exit in Las Vegas has to be one of the lowest moments - even if the intricacies of this track make it a bit of an outlier.

Charles Leclerc made a mistake at Turn 7 and failed to get a second lap in, while Lewis Hamilton didn't look convincing from FP3 onwards.

Leclerc was quick to point out the mistake was "following a lot of frustration, building up with a lot of mistakes with the way we managed" traffic, among other things, and said Ferrari might have been a victim of a GPS issue that hit during FP3.

He added that Ferrari had to be fully focused on gaining tyre temperature because that is the team's "weakness".

Giving a matter-of-fact take on where he thought Ferrari was losing out, Hamilton said: "It's a big chunk on the straights. It didn't feel like we had a tonne of grip. We were struggling to get the tyres working and we were just kind of nowhere."

His last lap was "very, very good", according to the team, so clearly it wasn't upset with the lap Hamilton put together.

And Hamilton reckoned losing a piece of his floor in Q1 cost him "three or four tenths" in downforce alone, while he also claimed a deployment issue was a big hinderance on his final Q2 lap.

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (1st)

It’s difficult to resist the Vegas gambling cliches when it comes to Antonelli's Q3.

He made the risky decision to back off at Turn 5 and drop to the back of the pack. Had he arrived at the line a couple of seconds later, he wouldn't even have been able to start his lap.

Instead, he made it just in time and found himself in the perfect place to pick up a monster, multi-car tow to the line at the end of the lap, setting the fastest time and minimising the pain of his five-place engine grid penalty brilliantly.

Albeit perhaps a touch fortunate, it was a good example of how beautifully Antonelli has played things throughout this year. Walking right up to the edge of disaster in order to crush everyone.

And from sixth on the grid, who would bet against him quickly getting himself amongst Verstappen and Russell in the race?

Loser: George Russell (3rd)

Antonelli's grid penalty will bump Russell up to second on the starting grid, but qualifying will feel like a missed opportunity given how strong Russell was in FP3, which he topped by nine tenths.

In fact, Russell actually ended up slower in Q3 than he'd been in FP3, left without the tow he pleaded for.

He diplomatically said "we'll take it offline, and we can talk about it" in the post-qualifying press conference, but he was clearly frustrated to have had his request denied.

Not least because it led to him being beaten to (an inherited) pole by the driver who has yet again infuriated him.

Winner: Max Verstappen (2nd)

Despite reporting "some weird issues" with his Red Bull, Verstappen did enough to be the fastest of the unpenalised drivers.

He wasn't sure if those issues will hamper him over a race distance - as they did at Austin - but he is well poised to fight for a fourth victory in six races and continue to set himself up as Antonelli's biggest 2027 threat.

Loser: Alpine (9th & 10th)

Did Pierre Gasly's eye-catching second place in Q2 have him dreaming of another challenge for pole position, a la Monza?

Gasly didn't say as much, but what came next was undoubtedly a disappointment. Even if it was unrealistic to expect a challenge for the top positions, replicating his Q2 lap would've put Gasly fifth in Q3, and fourth on the grid with Kimi Antonelli's penalty.

Instead, the prep lap didn't go to plan and, with cold tyres into the first corner, "two, three tenths" were lost in the first sector and the lap was gone, leaving him behind both Racing Bulls drivers and ahead only of team-mate Franco Colapinto - who was lucky to escape brushing the wall without more severe consequences.

It's the sort of turn of events that sums up Alpine's pursuit of Racing Bulls in the second half of the season.

Winner: Arvid Lindblad (6th)

Arvid Lindblad already bagged his best qualifying of the year and will benefit further from Antonelli's grid penalty to start fifth.

Lindblad's put in plenty of very strong qualifying laps this year - including in the last few races, which, he says, we haven't seen due to different things impacting his results - but even he wasn't sure this would be up there with his best.

"It was such a mess, the tyres weren't working, so I had a lot of understeer, I made a bit of a mistake in Turn 8, so it wasn't a perfect lap," Lindblad explained when asked by The Race whether it felt like one of the more special laps of his season.

"But also at the same time, there's a lot that's not gone my way the recent races, that's been out of my control."

Liam Lawson will start two places further back, as the Racing Bulls duo again outqualified the two Alpine drivers they're fighting for fifth in the constructors' championship. Lawson gave Lindblad a tow in Q2 which "I don't think it was entirely needed, but grateful", Lindblad summarised.

Loser: Haas (17th & 22nd)

Haas came into Friday hoping to get both cars into Q2 and using the heavily penalised Ollie Bearman to tow Rafael Camara to a better grid position.

But its first taste of slick-tyre running meant those expectations were quickly readjusted.

"Unfortunately, we weren't quick enough. We showed that in FP3," said Bearman. "So, yeah, I didn't get to set a lap, I was just trying to help Rafa to come through. It would have been too difficult basically to get both cars into Q2."

It was too difficult, it turns out, to get even one car into Q2 - despite Bearman doing "an amazing job", per 17th-place qualifier Camara, who said he "couldn't ask for more" from his team-mate.

Throw in a weird Bearman spin at the first corner in FP3 - in his words, to do with Haas's "quali engine map and how the rear brakes basically interact with the MGU-K" - that was effectively replicated by Camara in Q1, and this added up to Haas's most difficult day, performance-wise, for some time.

items.title: Verstappen responds to Russell after Las Vegas GP practice clash over 'gentleman's agreement'
Game Preview: Knicks vs Trail Blazers, November 21, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
As we all know, Madison Square Garden isn’t just the most glorious gymnasium on the planet and revered in the world of sports; it’s also famous for the long list of famous musicians who have performed under its unique bicycle-wheel ceiling. Now the Portland Trail Blazers are dropping by for a quick game of hoops on Saturday night, but they might actually be the one franchise that would be adept at bringing out the microphones as well. I mean, who wouldn’t want to hear the newest rendition of all-timers like or ?!

Not to disappoint anybody, but the days of Terry Porter and those shiny lycra dance outfits of the Blazers cheerleaders that would have made Cory Everson proud are long gone. Today’s Rip City Rascals (coming in at 10-5) have their own way of entertaining a crowd, though, which is more than many would have expected before the season. With the return of Damian Lillard and a highly questionable move for “Pistol Petey” Ja Morant, the Blazers looked to be about five years late to the modern NBA party but atleast early it turns out they are anything but.

Portland is fun under new coach Micah Nori

New head coach Micah Nori is making one of the more funky-looking rosters in the Association work so far, and he does it with a very modern, analytical approach. The Blazers shoot and make way more threes than their opponents (outscoring them by about 12+ points from beyond the arc), defend downtown better than 25 other teams in the NBA, and make sure Tony Brothers and his brothers-in-arms in the striped shirts have a living by drawing the second most fouls in the league.

Most of those foul numbers might be attributed to Deni Avdija. Only Luka from the Lakers and that feaky Greek in Miami stand at the charity stripe more frequently than the Israeli All-Star from Portland, leading to some fans questioning the ethics in his basketball bravado. But make no mistake about it, he is a serious talent, big-bodied and confident with a well-rounded game that can give every opponent problems. If he will be of any concern to the Knicks is not clear yet though; Avdija missed Portland’s last two with a foot injury and figures to be a game-time decision.

But even without Avdija, Portland (road record 7-3) will present a very interesting matchup for your Knickerbockers. Damian Lillard seems to be rejuvenated after his Achilles injury, and a lot about his game feels a bit more wholesome in the jersey in which he always belonged. Behind him you have a Jrue Holiday coming off the bench, probably one of the more professional, classy guys you can find in the NBA these days. Cheekily, he also still packs quite a punch in his game, giving Nori first-class playmaking, tough D, and leadership in spades. If you think rattling these two old wily pros might get you anywhere, think again.

Superior depth could be a factor for Knicks

You could have more luck with some of the younger Blazers, but many of them bring certain elite skills to the table, too. Belgian baller Toumani Camara is one of the best defenders in the entire league, long, lanky, and extremely athletic. Seemingly plodding big man Donovan Clingan is getting more mobile by the minute and still hasn’t lost his knack for gobbling up boards like a motivated Moses Malone did back in the day. Sidy Cissoko is another promising young wing, and former number two overall pick Scoot Henderson, while having a nightmarish season overall, can still break out for a big one as he did against Milwaukee the other night with 27 points.

What all those Blazers have in common is that they buy into Nori’s system so far and operate with a clear-cut plan on the shiny hardwood. They extend their defense, making it hard to find anything downtown but also possible to do some damage in the midrange. On offense, they move the ball well, play five-out as much as they can (using Clingan as a high screen setter), and rely on balanced scoring night in and night out. It’s a good formula, especially without Ja Morant, who has missed all but four games with a hamstring injury so far this year. The Knicks will have to touch the paint plenty to get that Portland defense moving, and they have to attack Lillard whenever possible on that end. Their superior depth could be a factor as well.

If the Blazers then throw a curveball and try to actually upend the Knicks’ three-game winning streak by dragging them into a singing competition after all? No need to worry – we still got !

Who: Portland Trail Blazers (10-5) at New York Knicks (9-6)Date: Saturday, November 21, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, New York, NYFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

items.title: What explains Ferrari’s worst F1 2026 qualifying
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Ferrari braced for a tough time on the long straights of Las Vegas, but neither driver making it into Q3 marked its worst qualifying showing of the Formula 1 season so far.

Charles Leclerc had wrecked his chances when he was forced to abort his second Q2 run after a mistake at Turn 7. He ended up 11th fastest (he starts 10th thanks to Oscar Piastri's penalty), while right behind him Lewis Hamilton was not helped by deployment problems and some car damage that he picked up in Q1. 

But Ferrari’s problems ran much deeper because a combination of its lack of top speed allied to the ongoing issues its drivers have faced in firing tyres up for qualifying that consigned them to their fate.

And, as Leclerc openly admitted when he spoke to the media after qualifying, the error he made in T7 was a consequence of growing annoyance at the lack of pace and ongoing communication problems with the pit wall.

“I think that is following a lot of frustration, building up with a lot of mistakes with the way we managed everything, traffic and other things,” he explained. 

“That doesn't help, particularly on a track like this where it's all about tyres. You've got to put tyres in the right window.

“I was more looking in my mirrors and trying to understand the traffic myself, that it makes it very difficult to do anything.”

Ferrari's well-known power unit weakness was particularly costly in Vegas.

“I'm just very disappointed,” he said. “We were expecting, and we lost one second down the straight - which is crazy. It's expected, and that makes it very, very difficult.

“On a track like this, it's the most power-sensitive track of the season, so we expected to have a hard time. But I was expecting to go through Q3.”

Hamilton said Ferrari wasn't blind to Las Vegas being a more challenging weekend, but he agreed the outcome was worse than anticipated.

We knew long straights and stuff was going to be challenging, but the gap seems to be a little bit more than I anticipated in the straightline,” he said.

“It's not insignificant. It's a big chunk on the straights. And then I don't know, just grip-wise, it didn't feel like we had a tonne of grip. We were struggling to get the tyres working and we were just kind of nowhere." 

Hamilton felt, however, that even in spite of the tyre and top speed problems, the potential was still within the car to make it to Q3 – taking into account the aero deficit from damage and energy management issues.

We lost a piece of the floor on the first or second lap of Q1. The car balance shifted and we lost three or four tenths [points] of downforce,” he said. “After that we were struggling more so with sliding, basically from the get-go.

“My lap was really good at the end, but I did the best I could with what I had. But then we lost something like six tenths just in deployment. I think without that we would have been in Q3. But otherwise, I was happy with my lap.” 

Another element that came under the spotlight was how the team executed qualifying, as Ferrari struggled for track position and didn't elect to play the slipstream game that many others were doing. 

Leclerc said that Ferrari had not gone down that route because it did not think a good tow would offer anywhere near the benefits of having tyres in the perfect operating window, considering how much it has struggled this year in managing its rubber.

“I mean, that was not discussed,” he said. “We thought that tyres were just everything. Keeping just the temperature in the tyres was the most important for us.

“We know it's our weakness. We've got to push. Even in the cool-down laps, we've got to push to keep the tyres high.

“I don't know if the others are facing the same issues as we do, but when you have that problem, then it's very difficult to wait for two cars, and to time it well, because that requires you to go slower than what you can. It's very, very tricky for us to keep those tyres up.”

There were also communication problems again with traffic management, but Leclerc wanted to understand better if GPS problems the team had suffered in practice had played a part in making things difficult in qualifying.

“I don't know what was the reason for that today,” he said. “I know this morning we had a lot of problems on GPS. If that was a problem today, then it's understandable.

“Otherwise, we just need to make sure that in those critical moments we get everything right. 

He added: “If it's a GPS issue, which doesn't necessarily come from us, then it's something that we cannot do much, and today was painful. 

"But if it comes from us, I do agree we need to look at it and obviously improve, because particularly in the critical moments like this, we need to be there, and we didn't.”

items.title: How to follow Las Vegas Grand Prix on the BBC
items.content: <article>All the key BBC coverage details for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, which takes place from 20-22 November.</article>
items.lbText:
The final triple header of the 2026 Formula 1 season starts in the United States with the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Lando Norris claimed his third victory of the season last time out in Sao Paulo, beating the Red Bulls of Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar.

With the drivers' championship already won by Kimi Antonelli, second place in the standings is still up for grabs.

Verstappen holds that position and is 17 points clear of George Russell, who moved back up to third place and one point ahead of Lewis Hamilton following his P4 at Interlagos.

Mercedes were also crowned constructors' champions in Brazil to move level with Williams on nine titles.

Lights out for Sunday's 50-lap race on the Las Vegas Strip is at 04:00 GMT (20:00 on Saturday local time).

Commentary of the race will be available across BBC Radio 5 Live, 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

You can also ask your smart speaker to "play 5 Live", for example.

Make sure to listen to every episode of the Chequered Flag podcast. For the first time this year, the post-race show for every grand prix is available to watch on BBC iPlayer and YouTube. , external

First practice: 00:30-01:30 - 5 Sports Extra

Second practice: 04:00-05:00 - 5 Sports Extra

Third practice: 00:30-01:30 - 5 Sports Extra

Qualifying: 04:00-05:00 - 5 Sports Extra

Race: 04:00 - BBC Radio 5 Live with build-up from 03:30

The weather forecast for Las Vegas looks dry and settled across the three days of track action.

Saturday's qualifying session and Sunday's grand prix both take place at night on the famous Strip, with conditions set to be clear with light winds and temperatures about 12C.

Much still to do on F1 diversity - Hamilton

Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?

items.title: Floor damage, deployment down to Hamilton's Las Vegas GP Q2 exit
Russell slams Verstappen after Las Vegas GP practice clash: ‘He walks around like he’s bigger and better than everyone’
Russell won't accept being 'screwed over' by Verstappen
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
George Russell has accused Max Verstappen of “walking around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else” after they clashed in practice at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Russell and Verstappen banged wheels at Turn 14 during FP3 with the stewards issuing Verstappen with a warning for moving under braking.

Neither was impressed and both were clearly still frustrated with the incident after a qualifying session that ensured they’ll share the front row together in Las Vegas, with Verstappen moving up to pole thanks to Kimi Antonelli's engine penalty.

With Russell second, the duo will likely face off into Turn 1 in the grand prix proper.

“I think a warning was fine. There's nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting a lap, but when you do this, you are screwing this person over, and he does this week in, week out with many drivers, and everybody accepts it,” Russell told Sky Italia.

“I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this, and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else.

“So, yeah, somebody's got to stand up to that guy.”

Russell and Verstappen have history as Russell claimed Verstappen said he was going to “put me on my f***ing head in the wall" before the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix after Verstappen lost pole position to a grid penalty for impeding Russell.

Both drivers were asked about the latest incident in FP3 in a clearly frosty post-qualifying top-three press conference, with Kimi Antonelli dividing them.

“Nothing happened” Verstappen simply said when asked about it, while Russell said “no confusion, it was pretty clear I think”.

The FIA announced earlier in the Vegas weekend that F1 would use full-time professional stewards for the first time from 2027.

Russell called that move “fantastic”, saying “Formula 1 was probably the only high-level sport that would have volunteer referees or stewards…there's a lot of stewards that are great at what they do but when there isn't the consistency everybody interprets a situation very slightly differently.

“If you have the same three same four week in week out we'll all know what what they're thinking. I'm very glad to hear that's come to fruition.”

items.title: Antonelli fastest but penalty leaves Verstappen on pole
items.content: <article>Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty hands pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.</article>
items.lbText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty will hand pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Antonelli, running at the back of the pack of cars in qualifying and maximising his tow, beat Verstappen by 0.258 seconds.

But the new world champion has a five-place grid penalty for using more than permitted number of engine components and will start sixth.

The Italian's team-mate George Russell was just 0.073secs behind Verstappen and will start alongside the Dutchman on the front row.

McLaren's Lando Norris qualified fourth, and will start third, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

Both Ferraris were eliminated in the second session and qualified 11th and 12th with Charles Leclerc ahead of Lewis Hamilton.

Each will be promoted a place by a 10-place penalty for McLaren's Oscar Piastri, who qualified seventh.

Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad, sixth fastest, is the last driver to be promoted as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh with Alpine's Pierre Gasly eighth and Franco Colapinto ninth.

Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar

Antonelli's final run did not start auspiciously as he and Russell became tangled up with the Alpines and Racing Bulls as they sought the best track position to optimise the slipstream effect.

Antonelli ended up the last driver to run and made it to the line with only one second to spare before the chequered flag, one second behind Lindblad.

Normally, being so close to the car in front would be a compromise but in Las Vegas it magnified the tow effect and Antonelli leapt to the front. "That was all the tow," he said over the radio after being told he was on pole.

"Starting the lap, I was only one second behind the car in front and I thought I was screwed," he said. "But the tow is so powerful here."

Verstappen, who has won two of the three Las Vegas Grands Prix, said: "I have been struggling with some weird issues that were also in the car in Brazil and just trying to get my head around how to deal with that.

"In qualifying we managed to make it work. Had a solid qualifying. My first lap in qualifying was pretty much as good as it could be with the tow, so to be on the front row is good for us.

"It was solid in the corners, and you have a bit of dirty air, but it is insane how much you gain on the straights."

Russell had looked in the running for the pole, but was happy with his session despite missing out.

"Overall it's been a very solid session and a solid day," he said.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance than in Mexico when I was on the front row.

"Kimi did a great job and he probably thought it wasn't going to work out so well being so close but with the tow it worked out."

Leclerc and Hamilton were separated by 0.056 seconds and both had tales of woe that explained their early exit - but very different ones.

Leclerc said: "Just a very poor qualifying. We are losing one second in the straights which makes it difficult enough already, and then I did a mistake when I had to put the lap in in Q2, following multiple mistakes we have done as a team and this we need to look at because it builds a lot of frustration that doesn't help.

"But in the end the mistake is on me and I will look at that."

Hamilton added: "It was a nightmare. Just low grip, felt like the tyres weren't working, had some damage on the floor that appeared out of nowhere and was losing 0.3-0.4secs and then had a deployment issue that lost us 0.6secs and with that we were nowhere, and I had no-one ahead of me. That wasn't great. So everything wasn't great.

"We knew we would struggle a bit here but maybe more than we anticipated."

items.title: Penalised Antonelli beats Verstappen with both Ferraris out in Q2
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Kimi Antonelli topped qualifying at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, but Max Verstappen will start from pole position because of the Mercedes driver’s grid penalty, and both Ferrari's failed to make the pole fight.

Antonelli has a five-place grid penalty for taking the updated Mercedes ADUO turbocharger this weekend, but he minimised the damage of that beautifully in Q3.

Antonelli gambled by dropping back from a squabbling pack of cars on the final runs as he ended up crossing the line with only a couple of seconds to spare.

But that turned out perfectly as he was in the ideal track position to pick up a huge slipstream from multiple cars at the end of the lap to set a 1m33.893s.

That was two and a half tenths quicker than Max Verstappen, who couldn’t improve on his second Q3 run.

But he’ll start from pole position because of Antonelli’s penalty and will share the front row of the grid with the man he clashed with in practice, George Russell.

Russell asked Mercedes for a tow from Antonelli, which didn’t transpire.

Lando Norris was fourth for McLaren ahead of Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls, who was a career-best sixth.

Oscar Piastri was seventh but he has to serve a 10-place grid penalty.

Liam Lawson was eighth ahead of Alpine’s Pierre Gasly, who had been second in Q2. Team-mate Franco Colapinto rounded out the top 10, after brushing the wall.

The biggest shock of qualifying proved to be a double Ferrari Q2 elimination, the first time the team has failed to get a car into Q3 since Imola last year.

Lewis Hamilton was struggling throughout FP3 and qualifying, and looked vulnerable to an early exit from the start.

But team-mate Charles Leclerc ended up joining him in the danger zone after he made an error into Turn 7, ruined his lap and then fell short of making the chequered flag for another attempt.

As others improved, that meant Leclerc and Hamilton were shuffled down to 11th and 12th.

Behind them were the Audis and Williams, with Nico Hulkenberg leading Carlos Sainz, Gabriel Bortoleto and Alex Albon.

Rafael Camara was knocked out in 17th in his second-ever F1 qualifying session, seven hundredths away from a second successive Q2 session.

Sergio Perez was 18th for Cadillac - his best qualifying since Monaco - even though he was left without a tow from his team-mate Valtteri Bottas on his lap, as in Bottas’s words, “We lost each other.”

Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll were 19th and 20th for Aston Martin, ahead of Bottas and Bearman, who sacrificed his qualifying session to tow Camara, because of his huge grid penalty.

items.title: Yankees news: Loáisiga back; Gil, Cruz cut loose
items.author: Nick Power
items.content:
MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: As John covered yesterday morning, the Yankees have brought Jonathan Loáisiga back into the fold, securing another deal with a familiar face in the early days of free agency to augment their bullpen. The 32-year-old agreed to a two-year, $18 million contract with a club option for 2029.

Loáisiga spent eight years in pinstripes, making 193 appearances while struggling to stay healthy. He returned to form in a major way in his sole season in Arizona last year, posting a 2.42 ERA in 67 innings. The right-hander pitches off an exceptional sinker, which sat at 97.9 mph last year and helped him to an elite 55.8 percent ground-ball rate (though he uses the sinker a little less than his peak Yankees days). Loáisiga joins the re-signed David Bednar and Tim Hill as bullpen fortifications, with fellow free agent Paul Blackburn another name linked to New York.

MLB Trade Rumors | Anthony Franco: The offseason giveth, and the offseason taketh away. The Yankees parted ways with a pair of pitchers Friday, choosing to non-tender Fernando Cruz and Luis Gil. Each was projected to earn $2.3 million in arbitration. Cruz was a top late-inning option the past two seasons but suffered a partially torn UCL down the stretch last year. For the Yankees, that injury and the fact that Cruz will turn 37 in March made him expendable. For Gil, who won the AL Rookie of the Year in 2024, it was a precipitous fall from grace. Shoulder injuries and ineffectiveness limited the right-hander to 20 appearances over the past two years and, despite the fact he’s still only 28, the Yankees felt Gil no longer had a future in pinstripes.

The Yankees did tender contracts to their other six arbitration-eligible players: José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Clarke Schmidt, Anthony Volpe, Ryan Weathers and Austin Wells.

FanGraphs | Davy Andrews: The signings of Loáisiga and Hill continue the Yankees’ trend of prioritizing ground balls over strikeouts from their bullpen arms. Hill’s is an extreme case — the southpaw comfortably led baseball with a 68.8 ground-ball rate but got torched when opponents did put the ball in the air, allowing homers on nearly 31 percent of fly balls. Loáisiga’s arsenal was tweaked by the Diamondbacks last year; his four-seamer, previously an afterthought, became a viable third pitch against which opponents hit .148. He also regained speed on his fastballs, perhaps the most critical element in his resurgence.

MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: For the 15th year, Brian Cashman participated in the Sleep Out, spending a cold November night outside in a sleeping bag to raise money for Covenant House, a non-profit that provides support for unhoused youth. He does this despite the many memes it inspires of the Yankees GM sleeping on the job, telling the , “I’ll take all those shots for a good cause.” During the event, Cashman gave some updates on the free agency process, which he equates to “drinking out of a fire hose right now,” due to the rush to make acquisitions before the looming lockout. He celebrated the re-signing of Bednar and Hill to fortify the bullpen, acknowledged he’s “having conversations” about upgrading at third, and declined to anoint Spencer Jones as the presumptive starter in center.

MLB Trade Rumors | Charlie Wright: Another topic of conversation at the Sleep Out was Jasson Domínguez. Cashman noted that the Martian is “pounding the ball in winter ball,” adding that he’s been fielding calls about the 23-year-old former phenom. It remains to be seen what the Yankees GM would be looking for in an exchange for Domínguez, who has disappointed early in his MLB career but still features an enticing raw skill set. The outfielder has a 1.069 OPS with seven extra-base hits and 12 RBI in 12 Dominican Winter League games.

FanGraphs | Eric Longenhagen: FanGraphs released their updated rankings of the Yankees’ top 37 prospects Friday. The upshot is that the system is below average overall and particularly threadbare among position players. The Yankees have more promising pitching talent, as eight of the team’s top 10 prospects are hurlers. Topping the list, though, is shortstop Dax Kilby. Evaluators love the 20-year-old’s swing and defensive profile; his ascent has been slowed by injury but Longenhagen suggests a “Gunnar Henderson-esque turn” is within the realm of possibility. Carlos Lagrange and Elmer Rodríguez follow as the top pitching prospects.

FanGraphs | David Laurila: The number-28 prospect on the list, Antonio Gomez, made a fortuitous decision before the start of the 2026 season. A strong defensive catcher whose offensive profile had stalled out, the Yankees farmhand flipped to the other end of the battery. The early returns from the mound have been strong; the 25-year-old features a four-seamer sitting in the high 90s, a sinker, and a slider, with encouraging control for a recent convert. Gomez’s 16.1-inning audition between A-ball and the Arizona Fall League are enough to encourage some evaluators to now consider him a legitimate prospect.

items.title: Why Verstappen escaped grid drop for Russell practice clash
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Max Verstappen escaped with a warning for his clash with George Russell in final practice at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Verstappen and Russell bizarrely banged wheels while going side-by-side through Turn 14 in the dying moments of FP3 and they had to see the stewards before qualifying.

Verstappen and Liam Lawson had been given a one-place grid penalty for a practice run-in in Mexico, but in Las Vegas, the stewards ultimately ruled that a warning for Verstappen was sufficient.

The stewards explained that “the drivers discussed the informal gentlemen's agreements concerning the preparation for a flying lap and the conduct expected between drivers in such situations" but decided "such informal understandings were of limited relevance to the assessment of the incident".

“The decisive considerations were the actual movements of both cars and their relative positions," the stewards document continued.

“The stewards therefore examined the braking and change of direction of Verstappen, the evasive manoeuvre and positioning of Russell and taking into account the applicable driving standards guidelines.

“The stewards considered that Verstappen’s change of direction under braking was unpredictable and contributed to the situation in which Russell had to move to the inside to avoid contact.

“While the stewards did not consider the manoeuvre sufficiently serious to warrant a more severe penalty, they concluded that changing direction under braking in these circumstances fell below the standard of driving expected.

“Taking into account the circumstances of the incident, the stewards determined that a driver warning was appropriate.”

Ultimately, the Las Vegas incident has been judged as a simple moving-under-braking offence.

The Mexico incident with Lawson resulted in grid drops because both drivers, in the words of the stewards, “behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable”, and it came directly after a warning to all teams to avoid such practice incidents.

No further action was taken over Verstappen’s other FP3 Vegas incident with Franco Colapinto’s Alpine because of “mitigating elements”, including Verstappen experiencing an engine issue earlier in the lap and Verstappen being surprised that Colapinto was overtaking him, given neither was on a push lap.

Elsewhere, Alex Albon was handed a reprimand for “unpredictable and potentially dangerous” movement in front of Isack Hadjar’s Red Bull in the same session.

items.title: Russell and Verstappen make contact in final Vegas F1 practice
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
George Russell was fastest in the final practice session at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, despite a bizarre late-session run-in with Max Verstappen. 

Russell and Verstappen were fighting tooth and nail into Turn 14 in the dying moments of the session and were quickly noted by the stewards, who will investigate the incident after FP3. 

Verstappen passed Russell, who then tried to re-pass Verstappen, with the duo banging wheels through Turn 14. 

Verstappen told his Red Bull team Russell “pushed me into the barriers”. 

That wasn’t the only incident in FP3, as the stewards are also investigating an incident between Verstappen and Franco Colapinto’s Alpine. 

Russell’s session-topping 1m34.041s was comfortably the quickest time of the session and the event so far, given FP3 was the first dry session of the weekend. 

World champion team-mate Kimi Antonelli was second fastest but 0.911 seconds slower than Russell. He’s taking a five-place grid penalty this weekend for taking the new ADUO turbocharger. 

On theoretical laptimes (combined using a driver’s best three sectors), Liam Lawson was actually second fastest, 0.618s slower than Russell’s theoretical best. 

In reality, Lawson’s fastest time was actually only seventh quickest, 1.361s off the pace.

Lando Norris’s McLaren was third quickest, 0.974s off, with Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari fourth and Colapinto’s Alpine an impressive fifth. 

Verstappen was sixth after his Russell run-in, ahead of Lawson, Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari (via a couple of off-track moments), Pierre Gasly’s Alpine and Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls.

Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar
items.content: <article>Formula 1 drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix.</article>
items.lbText:
Formula 1 drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed Lusail track, which has a series of demanding, long-duration corners.

It means teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix, as was the case last year.

The limit applies on a single set of tyres whenever it is used across sessions.

So mileage done in practice or qualifying, for example, would limit the number of laps that could be done on a set of tyres in the race.

Pirelli said the limit was longer then last year's 25 laps because of the reduced downforce levels of the 2026 cars compared with 2025.

"The increase has been made possible by the lower load levels recorded so far on the current generation of cars and by a further reinforcement of the tyre construction," a statement said.

Last year, the limit led to a major strategic error by McLaren, who lost a win because they failed to pit under a safety car period when everyone else did.

It is the third time in four years Pirelli has imposed a tyre-duration limit at Qatar, where running wide over flat kerbs in addition to the high-speed nature of the track is especially demanding for the tyres.

Pirelli described the decision as a "precautionary measure" that was "linked to the unique characteristics of the Lusail circuit, which is particularly demanding in terms of energy loads, thermal stress and tread wear".

In terms of the way the limit will be imposed, the statement said: "Laps will be counted cumulatively across all track sessions, including any laps completed under the safety car or virtual safety car.

"As far as the grand prix is concerned, all laps completed from the start signal to the chequered flag will count towards the total.

"Reconnaissance laps, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

"In all other track sessions, any lap that has been started but not completed will nevertheless be counted as a full lap.

"Should a team assemble a tyre set using tyres that have covered different mileages, the tyre with the highest lap count will determine the mileage attributed to that set."

Welcome to Velo Deals. We sift through the retail landscape to bring you deals worth paying attention to. It might be a discount or it might just be a product so good you should grab it. Either way, if it’s worth your time, you’ll see it here. If you’d like to see the rest of the category, check all our Velo Deals coverage.

When it comes to bike computers, the biggest players are Garmin and Wahoo, and each takes a fundamentally different approach to solving the same puzzle. If you want simple, Wahoo is the one for you, and all three size options are being offered at a massive discount right now.

Across the entire lineup, Wahoo makes the easiest-to-use bike computers on the market. They are the ultimate “it just works” devices: add your accounts, connect to Wi-Fi, and you’re ready to ride. You aren’t giving up serious metrics for that simplicity, either. Instead of painstakingly assigning data to individual boxes, you just list your fields in order of importance in the app and use the side buttons to zoom in or out on the fly. Even if you normally like a lot of data, it’s great to zoom in to just power and speed when it’s late in a ride, everything hurts, and you just need to pedal.

The main trade-off in the past was always that Wahoo doesn’t offer an all-encompassing 24/7 wearable ecosystem, but even that’s been fixed recently. Wahoo has a partnership with Coros, and if you want a full picture of both training and recovery, you can use the Coros backend system and a Coros watch seamlessly with your Wahoo computer.

At the top of the lineup sits the Elemnt Ace, which is Wahoo’s answer for riders who want maximum screen real estate and every feature the brand makes. It has a large 3.8-inch color touchscreen, 64GB of storage, dual-band GPS, a built-in speaker for voice turn-by-turn navigation, and up to 30 hours of claimed battery life. Its headline differentiator is an integrated wind sensor that measures live airspeed to quantify headwinds, tailwinds, and drafting. All of that hardware comes with a clear trade-off in size and weight—at 208 grams, it is noticeably larger and heavier than a standard head unit, which is why Wahoo includes an aluminum out-front mount in the box.

This is probably the one you really want. It keeps almost everything that makes the Ace appealing—including the 16-million-color touchscreen interface, 64GB of storage, dual-band GPS, and the built-in speaker for audible turn-by-turn prompts—while dropping the wind sensor and massive size. Instead of a 3.8-inch display, it steps down to a still very usable 2.8-inch screen and cuts the weight nearly in half to 109 grams, with a claimed battery life of up to 25 hours.

If you want something smaller and lighter for racing or just prefer a cleaner cockpit, the Elemnt Bolt 3 strips the formula down to the essentials. This is also the best budget play, but it’s still a very capable computer. Weighing in at 84 grams with a 2.3-inch color display, it drops both the touchscreen and the audio speaker, relying strictly on physical buttons for control. Storage drops to 32GB and claimed battery life dips to 20 hours, but you still get the same dual-band GPS, high-contrast color screen tech, and updated Ready-To-Ride interface found on its bigger siblings.

items.title: These E-Bikes Make City Riding a Joy
items.author: Alison Jaksen
items.content: With lightweight, minimalist design, Aventon’s new rides turn urban streets into your personal playground
items.lbText:
The Aventon Solterra 3. (Photo: Aventon)

Riding a bike, at its heart, is amazing because it’s so simple. Two wheels, a frame, and suddenly you’re zooming around and discovering that going places can be fun . That’s why fixed-gear and single-speed bikes have such passionate fans: They prioritize the freedom that comes from embracing simplicity. With less weight and extraneous features, biking reenters the realm of play, and a daily commute or jaunt to grab groceries can feel a lot like flying.

Enter Aventon’s Soltera 2.5 and Soltera 3 ADV, which capture that fixie magic. The brand launched its legendary fixed gear Mataró model back in 2013, and that minimalist spirit infuses this new pair of e-bikes. They both marry a light-is-right sensibility with powerful but barely-there motors, all of it in a stealth design that will change the way you think about e-bikes.

The Class 1 Soltera 3 ADV Ebike ($1,499) will delight purists. Powered by a 250-watt (500-watt peak) motor, it offers 40 Nm of torque and a 70-mile range in a featherweight 37-pound package. It swaps a clanky chain for a carbon reinforced polymer belt that’s way easier to maintain and can last two to three times longer than any chain. Its single-speed configuration keeps you nimble and agile in the stop-start flow and narrow corridors you’ll encounter in urban traffic.

The Soltera 3’s updated geometry sings in the concrete maze, too—and everywhere. A longer wheelbase and lower bottom bracket keep it planted and predictable at speed, while a taller stack puts you in a more upright position that’s easier on your back, wrists, and neck on longer rides. A lower standover makes it easy to hop on and off at every light. With its ease of use and maintenance, there’s no simpler way to get some electric oomph into your daily ride.

Want to go down the zen road of simplicity but retain a bit more flex and options? You want the Soltera 2.5 Ebike ($1,199). For a scant 9 more pounds, you get a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain, on-demand throttle, wired features, and a 46-mile range. It brings a more traditional city e-bike feel while paring away the fluff to maintain fixie-forward geometry and feel.

Swapping your trusty-rusty analog commuting horse for an e-bike can feel like settling for an underpowered motorcycle. But both Soltera models deliver electric power while reaching back to a style of riding with less weight, complication, and stress—and more of what you need to make city streets fun to ride.

Aventon Bikes is here to inspire adventures, both big and small, in all terrains of life. No matter what we look like now, a year from now, or a decade from now, this is what keeps us moving forward. Redefine adventure and learn more at aventon.com .

items.title: Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears £100m
items.content: <article>Manchester United borrowed £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino would be their new head coach, which will cost them £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United borrowed another £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach.

In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, United said they would be liable to pay £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer to hire the Argentine.

United announced Pochettino had agreed a two-and-a-half-year deal on 13 November. They borrowed £10m on 16 November.

The loan is one of three confirmed after the 30 September first-quarter reporting date, which takes the overall amount owed on their rolling credit limit to £240m.

The amount paid to release Pochettino from his USA deal takes the sums paid hiring and firing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 to £95m. However, that figure is likely to top £100m once the cost of hiring Pochettino's staff and sacking Michael Carrick is added.

Carrick was sacked last week with the club in the relegation zone and enduring their worst start to a season in 40 years. The former midfielder only signed a two-year contract in the summer after a successful six-month spell in caretaker charge last season.

Pochettino is the ninth full-time manager to be appointed since Ferguson, including Ralf Rangnick in November 2021. United have changed their manager in the middle of the last three campaigns.

The club also confirmed they had spent £5.7m to either acquire or extend registrations of "certain players and members of coaching staff".

The filing also revealed they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £181m of which is due after one year. United said on Thursday their substantial $750m debt was £577.4m when converted to sterling on 30 September.

items.title: Yankees non-tender Fernando Cruz, Luis Gil
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
The deadline to tender contracts to arbitration-eligible players arrived at 5pm ET on November 20th, and the Yankees have decided to non-tender Fernando Cruz and Luis Gil. The pair of right-handed pitchers become free agents, while Luis García Jr., Anthony Volpe, Ryan Weathers, Clarke Schmidt, Austin Wells, José Caballero, and Heliot Ramos have the next few months to decide whether to accept the Yankees’ offer or submit their own offers as the initial step in negotiating a salary for 2027.

Should both parties fail to agree on a number, the case would be submitted to an arbitration hearing. These hearings typically occur in February — subject to change due to the looming expiry of the CBA and expected owner lockout of the players — with the arbitration panel resolving the case by awarding the figure tendered by either the club or the player as opposed to a midpoint of those two figures.

The decision to non-tender Cruz and Gil does not come as much of a surprise. Both players were tabbed to earn $2.3 million in 2027 according to MLB Trade Rumors’ arbitration projections — an affordable amount that the Yankees nonetheless decided was better spent elsewhere given the question marks surrounding both players’ health and effectiveness going forward. It is the second year in the row that the Yankees have used the non-tender as a way to clear roster space on the pitching side. In 2025, they non-tendered five pitchers — Mark Leiter Jr., Ian Hamilton, Scott Effross, Jake Cousins, and Michael Arias — out of their 14 arbitration-eligible players.

Our own Andrés Chávez identified Gil as a non-tender candidate at the beginning of the month. It has been a precipitous fall from the stratospheric seven-start stretch that ultimately won Gil the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year Award. He has battled lat and shoulder injuries over the past two seasons, limiting him to 20 appearances (15 starts) with a 3.74 ERA, 5.44 FIP, and 58 strikeouts in 84.1 innings. An alarming loss of velocity on his fastball and worsening command has seen his strikeout rate crater from 27.3-percent between 2021-2024 to just 15.8-percent in the last two years, creating an untenable 1.9-percent strikeout-minus-walk ratio. There were question whether Gil might rediscover some effectiveness in a max-effort bullpen role, but ultimately the Yankees decided that the experiment wasn’t worth the effort. In five big league seasons with the Yankees, Gil went 21-11 in 56 appearances (51 starts), posting a 3.61 ERA, 4.54 FIP, 272 strikeouts, and 2.8 fWAR in 269.1 innings.

As for Cruz, the righty reliever became something of a cult hero thanks to his devastating splitter and enthusiastic celebrations. Arriving via trade from the Reds in the 2024-25 offseason, Cruz carved out a late-inning high leverage role by posting a 32-percent strikeout rate thanks to the splitter that allowed him to sit at the very top of the league whiff rate leaderboard. However, his appearances waned across his final two months of action in 2026, and it was subsequently revealed that he had suffered a partial tear of his UCL. The injury ended his campaign despite Cruz opting not to undergo surgery in the hope of making a late-season comeback. He was recently able to begin a throwing program, and GM Brian Cashman expressed optimism about his availability in 2027, but it appears the medicals on his elbow were scary enough to not be worth the risk at that price. In two seasons with the Yankees, Cruz made 110 relief appearances, pitching to a 3.33 ERA and 3.71 FIP with 139 strikeouts and 1.2 fWAR in 102.2 innings.

It is no surprise that the Yankees tendered contracts to the remaining seven arbitration-eligible players. The only other plausible candidate for non-tender was Schmidt, who is projected to earn $4.5 million in his third and final year of arbitration eligibility. The 30-year-old righty has missed significant parts of the last three seasons to injury — a lat strain in 2024, Tommy John surgery in 2025, and a biceps injury shortly after his return from Tommy John rehab in 2026. In total, he has made just 30 starts since the start of 2024, pitching just 164.2 innings after tossing a career-high 159 in 2023. However, Cashman confirmed that Schmidt is fully healthy entering this offseason, and the righty offers a much high floor and ceiling than Gil as starting rotation depth while also representing an intriguing multi-inning relief option.

With Cruz and Gil’s non-tenders, the Yankees have now subtracted two more arms from their already depleted relief corps. David Bednar did choose to return on the qualifying offer while the team has also reunited with Tim Hill and Jonathan Loáisiga in recent days, but there remains a good deal of work to be done to fill out the big-leaguer bullpen. There also remains the possibility that the Yankees could reintegrate Cruz and Gil on minor-league deals in the coming days.

items.title: One Editor Thinks 32-Inch Gravel Is the Future. Another Gives It Five Years.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Logan makes the case for bigger wheels, Mike blames bad geometry, Lisa sees a Big Wheel, and Blue Hat Guy puts a five-year expiration date on the whole standard.
items.lbText:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

This week, the full crew is together to do some arguing. Host Mike Levy, Lisa Charlebois, Logan Jones-Wilkins, and I (Josh Ross, though Blue Hat Guy works too) are debating Zwift versus everyone and whether 32-inch wheels are actually here to stay.

Before we get to the main event, we dive into a pile of listener comments from last week’s indoor riding and Zwift Plus discussion. That includes everything from TrainerRoad or Strava versus Zwift (and why fearing for life on rollers might be the best way) to whether Zwift will eventually fold Rouvy into a single platform. For the record, I’m putting my prediction on the board now: Rouvy ceases to exist as a separate thing in three years. We also tackle a listener theory that virtual cars in Zwift video routes are desensitizing indoor-first riders to real traffic—a take that leaves Mike and me pretty much speechless before Logan steps in with a much more reasonable explanation.

From there, it is time for the topic everyone loves to hate: 32-inch gravel wheels. Logan just wrapped up 500 miles on the MMosaic GT i55 32—a custom titanium bike built around a proper 32-inch carbon fork—and he is a huge fan. He argues it makes gravel riding noticeably more fun, with better rollover, more traction, and geometry that actually makes sense off-road. Mike agrees, arguing that the best thing about 32-inch wheels isn’t even the wheels themselves, but the longer, more stable geometry they force frame builders to adopt.

I am on the other side of the fence. While I don’t doubt the off-road performance gains exist, my argument is a business one: consumers have wheel-size fatigue, brands don’t want to manage multiple standards, and 32-inch gravel bikes are headed for the same fate as 650b within five years. That leads to a back-and-forth over whether brands can actually pull off two wheel sizes across a single frame run (when they still struggle to spec the right handlebar widths), whether 700c gravel bikes are just turning into “all-road” bikes, and what all of this means for shorter riders who don’t want to feel like they’re riding a monster truck.

Lisa: “This is gonna sound so dumb. I’m sorry, everybody. But it looks like you’re on a Big Wheel… It just looks so weird. The scale is so wrong.” Mike: “We all look so weird. We’re wearing spandex riding bicycles around, talking about watts and carbs. We look stupid and I love it.” Logan: “You know how many people noticed I was riding 32 at Big Sugar? Zero people. Nobody noticed.” Lisa: “Yeah, but you’re tall, dude. You look in proportion.”

As always, let us know where you land in the comments—are you with Logan on the 32-inch future, or are you siding with Blue Hat Guy? And make sure to vote in this week’s poll below to tell us whether you’re actually planning to buy a 32-inch gravel bike when they hit the market in force.
