items.title: Russell fastest in Las Vegas practice after rain
items.content: <article>Mercedes' George Russell topped a second practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix run on a wet but slowly drying track.</article>
items.lbText:
Mercedes driver George Russell topped a second practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix run on a wet but slowly drying track.

Russell, competing with Red Bull's Max Verstappen for second in the championship in the final three races of the year, set his time right at the end of the session.

The same applied to Alpine's Pierre Gasly, who went second, 0.071 seconds behind Russell, with a lap even later the Briton's.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, the main pace-setter throughout the session, was third fastest ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

The Frenchman had a faster lap ruined when he was blocked by Haas' Oliver Bearman at the end of the Strip.

Russell said: "We know in the wet it is different every lap, every session, realistically we were not the fastest today.

"McLaren looked exceptionally fast. Charles looked very fast at points, we just got the lap in when the track was at its driest and Norris didn't run.

"We have some things to understand because Kimi and I were very competitive in the wet last week and both of us were off the pace."

Hadjar added: "It was good fun but I don't think it's very useful for tomorrow. Just shaking down the car."

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was fifth, ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and the second McLaren of Lando Norris, who was fastest in the wettest early part of the session.

New world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest, ahead of Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.

F1 bosses close to V8 engines deal from 2030

The art of protection - inside an F1 helmet factory

Verstappen did not run until late in the session but was complaining about a problem with his engine.

Perhaps surprisingly given the conditions, the session was incident-free, although it was stopped briefly in the closing stages to recover a plastic bag that had blown on to the circuit.

Williams driver Alex Albon said: "I'm always surprised when I see no crashes. Trickiest track of the year, lowest grip of the year, these cars and a wet track is a lot of sliding."

The forecast is for dry weather for the rest of the weekend and the teams' focus will be on understanding the tyres, with warm-up so difficult in the cold conditions and with low loads going through the tyres.

This issue is exacerbated this year with the new 'straight-line mode', in which the wings open to reduce drag on the straights to aid energy recovery.

Russell said: "It's always a challenge here in Vegas but the added challenge this year with the nature of the cars, the SM zones everywhere, you're not putting any vertical load in the tyres so they are getting substantially cooler in the straight than in the previous years and they were already pretty cool."

In the first practice session, no driver completed a timed lap because the track was extremely wet and teams preferred to save their limited allocation of wet-weather tyres.

Hamilton said: "It wasn't a great day just sitting around waiting. You can't really test much in those conditions. And everything you learn from today you have to forget because tomorrow is supposed to be dry, so we kind of start from tomorrow.

"Everyone is (going in blind). No-one has put the slicks on, so we will have to react quickly. Hopefully, it's not bad and we are there or thereabouts."

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live and 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

Piastri will have a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine-part allowance this season.

The new internal combustion engine the Australian needs as a result of a failure at the Mexico City Grand Prix two races ago is his fifth of the season - only four are permitted.

Piastri and team-mate Norris will also use the latest turbo Mercedes have produced under F1's engine upgrade scheme but that comes penalty-free.

That is not the case for Williams' Carlos Sainz, who will take the new turbo but it is his fifth of the season, so he also has a 10-place penalty which team-mate Alex Albon avoids despite also fitting the new turbo.

At the factory team, only Antonelli will use the new turbo. The team decided it was not worth Russell having it as it would have given him a 15-place grid penalty.

The turbo provides only a small performance upgrade and is more aimed at expanding the engine's useability for the 2027 season.

Bearman also has a grid penalty for engine changes and is set to start from the back of the grid.

items.title: The art of protection - inside an F1 helmet factory
items.content: <article>Inside the extraordinary world of Formula 1 helmets, where precision engineering, personal expression and life-saving technology join forces.</article>
items.lbText:
As soft, instrumental opera music plays in the background of a precise temperature-controlled room in northern Italy, Thomaso is using a children's toy ball and hairdryer to perform his meticulous work.

Hugely focused, in a crisp white coat, he moulds a precious sticky black material over and over again for up to six hours.

One day, his fastidiousness may save the life of one of the best athletes in the world.

The room Thomaso works in is called "the magic shop". Its motto? 'One man, one shell.'

Much of what happens inside is top secret. What we can say is the black material Thomaso is working with is a blend of carbon fibre that has to be stored at exactly -16°C. He moulds it into a secret form, layer by layer, after which the entire unit is baked in a vacuum bag at a set pressure at 120C for three-and-a-half hours.

The handmade products he is working on are personally chosen by their clients - for their safety features, as well as comfort, practicality and look.

Thomaso's colleague Sven travels the world between February and December to keep those clients happy. A different country almost every week, with a reliable weather forecast almost as important as a large allowance of hand luggage.

Together with 32 colleagues, Thomaso and Sven work for one of the four leading manufacturers of F1 helmets.

They produce sophisticated engineering masterpieces, and works of art.

"Our philosophy is to make the best product for the best drivers," says chief executive Alberto Dall'Oglio.

In the early days of grand prix racing, protection was rudimentary. Drivers often wore little more than leather flying caps, goggles and - eventually - relatively basic open-face helmets.

Safety standards were inconsistent, materials primitive and the consequences of an accident frequently devastating.

According to the official F1 website, Giuseppe Farina - the first winner of an F1 race and first world champion - competed wearing nothing more than "his trusty cloth cap, two pairs of goggles (he wore the spare pair round his neck), cotton dungarees, leather boots and leather gloves".

The arrival of the full-face helmet in the late 1960s marked a defining moment. Bell introduced its pioneering Star model in 1966, and Dan Gurney became the first driver to race in a full-face helmet in 1968. The face - previously exposed to flying debris, fire and impact - finally had meaningful protection.

Progress was painfully slow, and motorsport's darkest moments repeatedly exposed the limitations of the technology.

In 1976, Niki Lauda 's Ferrari erupted into flames at the Nurburgring. His helmet came loose, leaving his head exposed to the fire. He survived, but suffered severe burns and lifelong injuries. The accident became a defining lesson in the importance of helmet retention, fire resistance and the protection of the driver's entire head.

The tragic deaths of Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna at Imola in 1994, followed by Jules Bianchi's fatal accident at Suzuka in 2014, demonstrated even increasingly sophisticated helmets could not eliminate every danger.

Ratzenberger suffered a fatal basilar skull fracture; Senna succumbed to multiple fractures of the skull base, after a strut from the suspension pierced his helmet.

Bianchi's accident exposed the vulnerability of drivers' heads to heavy external impacts. Helmets are only one part of a much wider safety system, which now includes stronger survival cells, the Hans device and the halo.

In 2004, the FIA introduced its new helmet safety standard, requiring advanced carbon-fibre construction to deliver greater strength, improved impact protection and reduced weight for F1 drivers.

At Bahrain's Sakhir circuit in 2020, Romain Grosjean's Haas split apart against the barriers and burst into flames. After 28 seconds trapped in the wreckage, he emerged with burns to his hands and ankles. His Bell helmet, fire-resistant equipment and the halo were instrumental in saving his life - a powerful testament to decades of safety innovation and engineering.

"Today's helmets are withstanding up to 30 seconds at 700, even 800, degrees," says Dall'Oglio. "Then they have to self-extinguish within 15 seconds."

Dall'Oglio is the CEO of Schuberth Performance, Thomaso an engineer and Sven a racing service technician, working trackside at more than 400 grands prix, preparing helmets and visors for rain, sun or floodlights.

Needing to avoid any impact on the helmets, he must carry them - sometimes five or six at a time - to races.

Schuberth, a German firm, has a long history in head protection. Founded in 1922, the company began making industrial products before moving into helmet linings in the late 1920s, then mining and motorcycle helmets in the 1950s.

With its HQ in Magdeburg and F1 helmet production in Schio, northern Italy, it produces special helmets for military forces - made of Kevlar, and some of a similar carbon - in the same factory as the F1 helmets.

Its motorsport credentials grew considerably around the turn of the millennium.

Following Michael Schumacher's British Grand Prix accident in 1999, Schuberth developed a new generation of racing helmets, subsequently worn by Schumacher and other leading drivers.

Of the current drivers, four-time world champion Max Verstappen is the most prominent to wear a Schuberth helmet. He is joined by Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar, Cadillac's Sergio Perez, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls.

Dall'Oglio's team hand-makes about 250 helmets a year.

An F1 helmet is a remarkable marriage of science and aesthetics.

Constructed using advanced composite materials, including carbon fibre, it must be exceptionally strong while remaining light enough to minimise strain on a driver's neck.

Visors, ventilation systems, fire-resistant linings, communication equipment, a straw-like drinks system and carefully designed retention mechanisms all contribute to its performance.…

items.title: Yankees news: MLB continues to frolic with private equity
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
Front Office Sports | Ben Horney: After the Yankees reached an investment deal with Apollo Global Management over the summer, the rapacious claws of private equity continue to sink into what was once the great American pastime. Swiss firm Seidler Equity Partners bought out an as-yet-undisclosed stake in Rawlings, the official baseball supplier to MLB, that the league has owned since 2018. MLB did say they would maintain “meaningful ownership” of the company, but it seems Seidler is the controlling partner. Expect offense to rise once the ghouls learn rubber is cheaper than leather.

NJ.com | Adam Zagoria: The Yankees have reportedly been in contact with Randy Arozarena’s camp, as the mercurial outfielder courts offers in his first true taste of free agency. The Yankees’ struggle from the right side of the plate was a story from the moment Aaron Judge went down, and in those dog days of summer where it felt like they faced a left-handed starter four out of five days, right-handed power would be an excellent add to the roster, and Randy’s never had a bad year at the plate. His defense and baserunning though…

Yahoo! Sports | Jackson Kruse: The Yankees made a small splash yesterday, inking switch-hitting outfielder Allan Castro to a minor league deal. Castro, just 23, became a minor-league free agent after playing in the Red Sox system since 2019, was a little underwhelming with an 88 wRC+ in 119 games for Triple-A Pawtucket, but per FanGraphs boasts above average power both raw and in-game. If the Yankees can build some kind of contact profile, he might end up a surprising depth piece going forward.

Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: Scenes from a beautiful game with a funky tail
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Timberwolves (11-5) have been the talk of the West, especially with their level of success given the absence of star guard Anthony Edwards (knee). Coach Chris Finch has his crew chucking up 116.7 points per game while also leading the league in rebounding and fielding the top defense. So far this season, the Wolves have held every opponent to under 50% from the floor—and they would again tonight. New York (9-6) knew the trouble that awaited them as they squared off with their first Western Conference team of the season. The game started with runs in either direction, but the Knicks gained steam and took a 15-point lead into halftime. In the third quarter, Minnesota chipped away at the lead, and Jaden McDaniels led the doggies on a rally in the fourth quarter to cut the lead to three with a scant few minutes left. But neither team could buy a bucket down the stretch. The Knicks went scoreless for the final three and a half minutes, the T’Wolves missed on everything, and the visitors escaped with a 102-99 victory.

That’s the lowest score for the Wolves this season. Take a bow, fellas.

On a first-quarter drive, LaMelo Ball (your favorite Ball brother?) swiped an arm across Jalen Brunson’s face. Cap was rattled by it and subbed out around the nine-minute mark, giving Tyler Kolek an unusually early appearance. With Jalen out, the visitors went on a 12-0 run. The backup guard was terrific in his first-half play, dishing five dimes in seven minutes, a third of the team’s total, and leading a second unit that tallied 17 first-half points.

A game of runs! Minny responded with a 13-2 run that included Ball attacking the paint for points and Jaden McDaniels swishing from long range. McDaniels was Minnesota’s most efficient scorer in the half, putting up 11 points on perfect 4-of-4 shooting, including three triples (but also three costly turnovers). Returning the favor, Josh Hart dropped a triple that started an 11-3 run and gave New York a 33-26 lead at the break.

In the second quarter, KAT and OG Anunoby stepped further into the spotlight. They combined for 30 first-half points on 12-of-18 shooting. Karl sang beautifully on his former home court, scoring 17 points and hauling in eight boards in just 16 minutes; OG chimed in with 13 points and a pair of blocks. Jose Alvarado got a little run but was quiet in the quarter. In a nice return to form, Josh Hart added nine points on 3-of-4 shooting from deep, while steady-eddie Landry Shamet provided a major lift off the bench with 10 points and a team-best plus-17 in 17 minutes.

The T’Wolves have length that can really clog the lane, and that explains why Jalen Brunson managed just seven points on 2-of-8 shooting, with his two makes coming from the outfield. Against most teams, Cap performs his string music in the paint, but these Minnesota trees make for a dense forest. Also underwhelming: Mikal Bridges, who threw the ball at the basket just once in his 11 minutes before intermission. It’s sort of wild that the Knicks posted 65 first-half points despite getting only nine points from their starting backcourt.

Also weird: Rudy Gobert had just five points and one rebound in his first 15 minutes. In fact, the Wolves’ starting frontcourt of McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga, and Gobert combined for two rebounds. Believe it, Ripley! They weren’t the only stinkers on the home team. Ball, Kuminga, and Ayo Dosunmu combined to shoot 4-of-17 through the half. Minnesota shot a respectable 44% overall and 39% from three, but outside of McDaniels, nobody found much rhythm. With the Knicks shooting a blistering 57% from the field and an eye-popping 63% from deep (10-of-16), the good guys were ahead 65-50 at intermission.

In the third quarter, Brunson shouldered the load, scoring 14 points in the period, and Bridges showed up to sink a three and commit two thefts. Towns continued to crash the glass but cooled off somewhat offensively, as did OG. For the home team, Kuminga poured in 14 points, making two three-pointers while blocking three shots. The Wolves couldn’t put together a sustained run, though. Trailing 83-66 with around 3:30 left, they outscored our heroes 12-7, cutting the score to 90-78 at the break.

To start the final frame, Kolek converted a four-point play to give the guests a 16-point lead. But we never thought the Furballs would roll over and die—and no, they didn’t. As New York’s offense stalled (e.g., Towns missed four of five, which he redeemed with three stuffs), McDaniels, Trey Lyles, and the Wolves chipped away at the lead. After New York went ahead 97-85 with 7:56 remaining, Minnesota scored eight unanswered points, including a McDaniels three and a Ball pull-up triple, to cut the lead to four. The Knicks went nearly four minutes without scoring, prompting a timeout and the return of Bridges and Anunoby.

What makes tonight’s win most stunning is that New York managed to achieve it despite going scoreless over the final 3:26. During that grisly stretch, KAT copped a flopping tech, Gobert slammed an alley-oop, and Ayo buried a three, bringing the Timberwolves within three with 2:34 left. Brunson missed a pull-up jumper, New York committed a shot-clock violation, Towns was called for an offensive foul with 1:04 left, and Bridges missed a turnaround jumper with 23 seconds remaining.

The hosts had plenty of chances to tie or steal the lead but couldn’t capitalize. Ball bricked two shots in the final 1:39; Dosunmu whiffed a bunny; and Bridges blocked Gobert’s putback attempt with 44 seconds left—arguably the biggest defensive play of the game. Ball blanked on a potential tying longball with 10 seconds remaining, and Kuminga collected the rebound but threw the ball away, with Landry Shamet securing the steal to end Minnesota’s night.

For those keeping track at home, the Timberwolves missed their final six field-goal attempts and committed five turnovers over the last five minutes. That’s a lot of ugly basketball to taint what was otherwise a quite pleasant viewing experience. But a win’s a win! And this one came over a very worthy opponent.

The Knicks host the Blazers on Saturday. Mo is sewing arms and legs onto your recap. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

State Has a $1,500 Gravel Bike With Real Progressive Geometry and Big Tire Clearance
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The alloy bike brings tons of value to modern gravel dimensions, while State has improved some of its more finicky budget components.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Today, State is launching the 6061 All-Road V2, and it packs a ton of value into an alloy frame. Of course, the price jumps out as the biggest draw, but the bike also brings 55mm of clearance, improved componentry, and truly progressive geometry. Progressive geometry that many big brands say they provide, yet ultimately don’t quite hit.

For State, this new geometry is built around stability and traction, complete with a slightly slacker headtube angle, a long 445mm chainstay length, and a 73mm bottom bracket drop. State also tweaks the geometry on a size-by-size basis, which aims to maintain similar handling across the size run. Crucially, for the smaller sizes, this size-based geometry is designed to reduce toe overlap—even for 55mm tires on a 48cm frame.

The 6061 All-Road v2 is firmly pitched as a budget bike that brings costs down through components and materials, yet tries to bring quality through intentional design. That is where those aspects of geometry have come in.

Since the bike is not race-focused, that has given State the license to zero in on a geometry that boosts stability through the front and rear of the bike. Instead of packing big tires into a short chassis, State took a chance to push the expectations around head tube angle and chainstay length. This length, specifically the head tube angle ranging from 70-71.5 degrees and a 445 mm chainstay, is going to add stability—especially with the larger tires—and is designed to balance weight distribution for better traction. These attributes make a ton of sense for an entry-level bike.

Nevertheless, viewing this as an entry-level bike does do a bit of a disservice to how this bike could grow with a rider. From aspects like a T47 bottom bracket to relatively aero-shaped tubing with semi-internal cable routing, the bike could be upgraded easily.

Like all of State’s budget builds, part of how the brand finds savings is through building bikes with drivetrain components from outside of Shimano and SRAM. In the past, this has led to some, erm, creative component selection.

One of the most frustrating examples of this, in my experience, was a hybrid braking system that combined cable-actuated levers with a hydraulic caliper. It created one of the most disjointed, frustrating brake systems I have ever used, but it’s gone. On this new build, the system is a full flat-mount hydraulic system that should make for much more consistent and digestible riding.

There are still quirks like a Sensah SRX Pro 1×12 rear mech and a State-branded 42t crankset, but the frame is both UDH-compatible and has reasonable 165mm cranks for the smaller sizes and 170mm for the larger frames. The bike also comes with the option to run both 700c and 650b wheel sizes.

Lastly, speaking of those wheels, State has an in-house 700c wheel option that has an updated 25mm internal width, 32-spoke count rim to suit the wide 50mm Continental Hard Pack tires that come stock with the bike. There is also the option to upgrade to the DT Swiss G 1800 or the Zipp 303 S XPLR wheelset.

The State 6061 All-Road v2 is available in three colors—Liquid Emerald, Chrome Red, and Metallic Smoke—and four sizes. The builds start at $1,499, with add-ons including wheels, pedals, saddles, seatpost, and bottle cages.

For more information or to configure yours, visit State’s website .

items.title: F1 to introduce full-time race stewards from 2027
items.content: <article>Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.</article>
items.lbText:
Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.

The move follows consistent calls from grand prix drivers for the change because of criticisms of inconsistency of decisions regarding penalties for on-track incidents.

The FIA said in a statement that it would begin recruiting permanent stewards, and was planning a "phased introduction" during the 2027 season.

The FIA statement added: "The introduction of dedicated full-time stewards to the FIA's flagship championship will provide continuity and expertise within the stewarding structure, further advancing the FIA's commitment to fairness through the ongoing review and continuous improvement of sporting regulations and stewarding guidelines.

"It will also allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making."

It said that the use of driver stewards, usually an ex-F1 driver, would continue, "recognising the invaluable expertise they bring".

The plan is for "a small number" of full-time stewards to be recruited during 2027 and the group to be expanded from 2028.

"Existing FIA stewards will continue to play a vital role, contributing their experience within a mixed roster of full-time and part-time stewards for the foreseeable future," the statement said.

In reality, the move is not a major step on from the current situation, where a small number of stewards are rotated around races.

Each grand prix has a group of four stewards, one of which is an ex-driver.

Current drivers have often referenced the fact that they had repeatedly complained during briefings with FIA officials that rulings on driver standards and racing errors were not applied on a consistent basis.

Last year, Williams driver Carlos Sainz, a director of drivers' body the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "F1 and the FIA all agree that [permanent stewards] should be the way forward, where at least two of the three stewards are permanent and we have one rotational for teaching purposes."

The decision follows the opening of an FIA race operations centre at F1's Biggin Hill headquarters in south London.

The FIA has in recent years received increased income from F1 - which provides the majority of its funding - on the basis that this would be applied to improving officialdom and rule-making.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

items.title: ‘It Would Be Great to Win All Three’: Chloé Dygert Dreams of Gold Medal Sweep at the LA 2028 Olympics
items.author: ahood
items.content: Chloé Dygert confirms to Velo she will target gold in road and track at the LA 2028 Olympics after her return to US pro racing.
items.lbText:
Dygert, second from left, was part of the gold medal-winning team in Paris. (Photo: Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

Chloé Dygert may be leaving the WorldTour, but she’s keeping her foot on the accelerator with an ambitious target of three medals at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics .

Dygert told Velo she’s aiming to defend Team USA’s team pursuit title and chase the time trial and road race at LA 2028.

With the Games less than two years away, the 29-year-old is already building toward a possible gold medal trifecta that could make her one of the breakout stars in Los Angeles.

“Of course it would be great to win all three, the time trial for sure, and then the road race would be just a total bonus,” Dygert told Velo . “I gotta be realistic here, so winning the time trial and obviously coming back and winning the team pursuit would be huge.”

As one of America’s most successful Olympic cyclists , Dygert already owns four Olympic medals. She won team pursuit gold and time trial bronze at Paris 2024, adding to her team pursuit bronze from Tokyo 2020 and silver from Rio 2016.

Qualifying comes first. Then she has to hit her peak across two disciplines in the summer of 2028.

Speaking to Velo’s Hannah Knapp at El Tour de Tucson, Dygert was already putting down some training sessions on the outdoor track.

“So for how the Olympics works, it kind of goes by body count rather than like the event itself,” she said. “I’m for sure gonna do the track team pursuit as long as we qualify and then hopefully the time trial and then by doing the time trial, I have to do the road race, so I’ll be doing three events.”

Two medals in Paris, so why not three in Los Angeles?

Dygert’s road to Los Angeles will run through the United States.

This week she confirmed she’s returning to Virginia’s Blue Ridge TWENTY28 after six seasons with Canyon SRAM in the WorldTour.

Dygert has been through the wringer with injuries and health setbacks. Her time trial crash at the 2020 world championships in Imola, where she suffered a devastating injury to her left leg, still divides her career into before and after.

“I’ve spent my time in Europe and gave it the best shot that I could. Before my accident, that was the plan,” Dygert said. “I wanted to go to Europe and I wanted to win everything in Europe. I wanted to be the best in Europe.

“But because of the accident, unfortunately some of those goals got derailed. I think it was very obvious that I just was never going to be the athlete that I was before the accident.”

Dygert returns to Nicola Kramer’s Continental team where she raced as a junior a decade ago.

“So now it’s all about what do I do going forward, how do I make the best of who I can still be, and that is why I’ve decided to come back to America,” Dygert said.

“I’m coming back to something that I’m familiar with, coming back to a team that supports me and my goals,” she said. “I want to win the worlds. I want to win the Olympics, and I’ve done that before with her, and so what a better team to come back to.”

Dygert is one of USA Cycling’s best shots at gold on home roads in 2028.

The two-time world time trial champion took bronze against the clock in Paris, and she heads into the Los Angeles Olympics with a title to defend on the track and a third chance at a medal in the road race. Here’s how all three stack up.

1. Defend gold in the team pursuit Dygert has been at the heart of the U.S. team pursuit for three straight Olympics, with a medal each time and a breakthrough gold in Paris. She skipped the track worlds last month, but told Velo the pursuit is still front and center in her plans for LA28.

Team USA has work to do. The Americans finished ninth in qualifying at the Shanghai worlds, more than three seconds shy of advancing. Kristen Faulkner was the only rider from the Paris gold medal quartet on the start line in China.

Only eight teams will start in Los Angeles. Great Britain won gold in Shanghai ahead of Italy and Germany, a reminder of how deep the field is. The Americans will have to earn their place first.

If they can find their Paris speed again, they’ll be in the medal fight.

2. Win gold in the individual time trial This is her other big target.

Dygert has won two world time trial titles, and she was less than a second from Olympic silver on slick roads in Paris. Grace Brown was in a league of her own that day, beating Dygert by more than 90 seconds. Just 0.87 seconds separated Dygert from silver medalist Anna Henderson.

The course will matter. Organizers have confirmed a start at the LA Zoo and a finish at Griffith Observatory, with the full route still to come.

How much climbing comes before that finish could shape Dygert’s chances of turning bronze into gold.

3. Take a shot in the Olympic road race First, Dygert needs a spot on the road team.

The United States has two guaranteed road race places per gender as host and can earn up to four per gender through the UCI nations rankings.

The road race is the longest shot, but Dygert has the engine for a long, hard race in national colors.

She finished 31st in the Olympic road race in Tokyo and 15th in Paris. She was fourth in 2019 and second at the 2024 worlds in Zürich to show what she can do when she’s in the mix at the finish.

Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
items.content: <article>Mauricio Pochettino's first Manchester United training session has been filmed by fan with a drone from outside the club's Carrington training ground.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.

Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.

Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.

"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.

"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."

The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."

Manchester United have declined to comment.

There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.

While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbuemo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, while neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season.

On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'Rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.

Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.

The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.

Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘It’s going to be bittersweet’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Revenge game for KAT today?

I don’t think so, but who knows.

Here’s the latest before visiting the Wolves in still-not-overly-cold Minnesota.

On Rick Brunson’s decision to bring Jose Alvarado into the game against Toronto:

“Just a great call. Rick Brunson made the call of throwing Jose in to see if he can give us a spark. So, just a heckuva call by Rick Brunson and just a fantastic job by Jose producing on both sides of the ball when his name was called.”

On Karl-Anthony Towns improving his passing decisions and avoiding risks:

“It’s a fine balance because he’s capable of making some beautiful passes in tight windows so you want to let him be him. But I thought earlier in the year — and we talked to him about it, and said it a couple times — he was trying to make the home-run pass a little too much.

“And he’s gotten to a point where he’s mixing it up now. We’re going to trust him because he’s obviously done it for many years now with good results. We’ll lean on him quite a bit in that regard but if we turn the ball over too much, we’ll let him know.”

On Towns’ basketball intelligence and ability to read the game:

“KAT’s got tremendous feel. He’s a smart, smart dude when it comes to a lot of things, but especially when it comes to the game of basketball.”

On Towns’ coachability and the impact of assistant coaches Brendan O’Connor and Darren Erman:

“It’s easy to see where he is, because everything we’ve asked him to do, he’s tried to do. So, you’re extremely coachable. You got a great feel. And you got two guys in (assistant coaches) Brendan O’Connor and Darren Erman that are teaching you the game defensively at a really high level, and you’re starting to see the results of it.”

On the Knicks’ execution and contributions throughout the roster against Toronto:

“Our execution was at an extremely high level. We had a lot of guys contribute in a lot of ways tonight.”

On the Knicks early-season woes:

“It’s still a work in progress.”

On why the NBA must continue penalizing dangerous closeouts and landing-space violations after Brunson’s injury scare:

“They got to keep track of it because it’s going to happen. Everybody wants to try to block [Brunson’s] shot and every other guy’s shot. Some guys go forward too much and, if they do, there’s got to be a heavy penalty. Because if there’s no heavy penalty, then guys won’t be conscious of it. They’ll just keep sliding underneath guys.”

On why his shooting technique sometimes exposes him to dangerous situations:

“I fade a little bit. Taller guys are usually guarding me, so I got to be able to fade a little bit. Sometimes they’re not jumping straight up. They’re jumping towards me. It happens.”

On prioritizing getting buckets over worrying about landing on a defender’s foot:

“I’m not worried about falling on his foot. I’m more worried about if he’s close enough to block it. If he is too close, I probably won’t shoot it. If he’s not, ball is going up.”

On the Knicks rediscovering their preferred style of play against Toronto:

“We just played to the best of our abilities. I know the early season hasn’t looked like it, but that’s how we’re most comfortable.”

On the disappointment of not winning a championship during his nine seasons in Minnesota:

“I wanted to win one there. I didn’t accomplish that. But it was great to have those moments, to bring Minnesota back to the playoffs and be able to do a lot of things.”

On returning to Minnesota as an NBA champion with the Knicks:

“It’s going to be bittersweet. I’m just happy that I have such amazing fans and had such an amazing time in Minnesota. I love it to death. I love that place so it’s going to be cool to go back.”

On becoming a minority owner of Napoli’s basketball team:

“Napoli is a great underdog story and reminds me of what we have built with the Knicks in many ways. It is a project built around hard work, big dreams and the incredible passion Napoli fans have for their team. I’ve been coming to Naples and the Amalfi Coast for years, and I know what a fan base like this can mean to a team. Seeing this club already making noise in the EuroCup tells you where it’s headed.

“Matt Rizzetta and the team at Underdog Global Partners have high ambitions with a real plan for where this club is going. The Napoli journey is still very much in the first quarter, so I am excited to be a part of building this into something truly special in the years ahead.”

On Instagram after being demoted from starting center to the second unit:

“Nobody gone save me, gotta save my damn self.”

items.title: Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, Paul Seixas among cycling stars set for audience with Pope Leo XIV
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
A host of representatives from the cycling world, including Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, and Paul Seixas, will attend an audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican next week.

UCI President David Lappartient described the November 23 event as "an opportunity to strengthen cycling's commitment, as a sport, to promoting peace and intercultural dialogue among peoples."

Past and present Grand Tour champions are among a group of over 100 "distinguished guests" attending, in addition to organisers of all men's and women's Grand Tours and other races, and representatives from various cycling federations.

Vollering, Merckx, and Seixas will be joined by a host of current and former road riders, including Bernard Hinault, Annemiek van Vleuten, Greg LeMond, Elisa Longo Borghini, Francesco Moser, Miguel Indurain, Jeannie Longo, Vincenzo Nibali, Chris Froome, and Mark Cavendish.

Multiple para-cycling world champion Ricardo Ten Argilés, multiple BMX world champion Mariana Pajón, and Ukrainian cyclist Anna Kolyzhuk, who suffered a serious spinal injury in a crash during a race this year, will also attend.

Ahead of the event, Lappartient "highlighted the longstanding historical roots between cycling and the Catholic Church, from races organised by parish communities and cycling teams inspired by Gospel values, to the various meetings with Popes throughout the 20th century and the recent passage of the Giro d’Italia through the Vatican during the 2025 Jubilee."

The event will see Pope Leo XIV take an audience with the riders before the UCI symbolically donates several bicycles to Caritas Rome, a charitable organisation founded by the Episcopal Conference of Italy.

The audience isn't the first time the Pope and the cycling world have come together. In 2025, the Pope blessed the peloton ahead of the final stage of the Giro d'Italia, which started in the Vatican. The stage was dedicated to Pope Francis, who died in April.

Several other Popes have addressed the Giro in the past, including Pope Paul VI in 1964 and Pope John Paul II in 2000. Pope John Paul II also offered his support to the Amore e Vita cycling team in the 1990s and 2000s.

items.title: Polygon’s Fastest Gravel Bike To Date
items.author: Alison Jaksen
items.content: Want to go fast and explore far and wide? The new Tambora is built for top-end speed over changing terrain.
items.lbText:
Polygon's new Tambora gravel bike. (Photo: Polygon Bikes)

Since 1989, manufacturing and development has been in Polygon Bikes’ DNA. The Indonesia-based factory brand is in a country shaped by tremendous geological forces. The island nation’s massive volcanoes have reformed the landscape countless times and created awe-inspiring topography.

The lesson: Change is good. Polygon focused on a clear priority with the evolution of the all-new Tambora: speed. This is the fastest gravel bike the company has produced, with design elements that let riders push their routes faster and further than ever. Compared to the previous version of the Tambora, the front end is 32mm lower, while the head angle slackens by 0.8 degrees. Those tweaks improve aerodynamics for both bike and rider, while the longer wheelbase and chainstays create more stability when you’re charging down the trail.

​Adding to the Tambora’s race-ready performance: its frame. The frame’s ACX carbon-fiber construction takes inspiration from its Helios road bike sibling—designed to excel at power transfer while reducing ride fatigue. The bike also boasts 55c tire clearance and is compatible with 1x and 2x drivetrains. If more rugged terrain calls to you, the Tambora is also compatible with aftermarket suspension forks up to 40mm of travel, without changing the current geometry.

​While speed is this bike’s specialty, it also features the thoughtful, rider-friendly design elements Polygon is known for. The new Tambora takes full advantage of the brand’s PolyPocket internal frame storage, which offers a full downtube width opening for easy access. This soft-sided, zippered pouch holds tools, snacks, and other essentials in a convenient, low-profile package. Up in the cockpit, a Fidlock mount recessed into the top tube makes it quick and easy to connect your preferred accessories, while keeping everything tight when you ratchet up the RPMs.

Also great: The value proposition for Polygon Bikes is as good as the performance. The Tambora series starts at $1,799, with a wide range of competitively priced options. The Tambora 7 Di2 ($2,999) and Tambora 9 AXS with SRAM Force ($4,499) are particularly good deals considering the specs.

Put it all together and you have a bike that’s both fast and capable of serious saddle time—and comes at sweet price. With four models across six frame sizes, there’s a redesigned Tambora for every gravel rider who wants to experience the wonders of evolution for themselves.

Founded in 1989, Polygon began with a simple belief: Great bikes shouldn’t be out of reach. What started as a small OEM operation has grown through decades of building, experimenting, and refining bikes for real riders—experiences that still define the global brand today.

items.title: ‘Should Manchester United fans be hoping for relegation?’ Will Unwin answered your questions
items.author: Will Unwin and Guardian moderators
items.content:
As Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge at Anfield, the Guardian’s Will Unwin answered your questions on Manchester United’s new head coach, the boardroom, the academy and whether Frank Ilett will ever get a haircut.

Every few months there is the report of a new “wonderkid” being signed: a South American full-back, a Scandinavian midfielder, a flying winger etc. But then they never seem to make the squad, let alone the first team. The same for our academy, which wins trophies regularly. Are there real prospects who could supplement or even improve the team? Is it too difficult to introduce them into Premier League games? Are they just investments for future sell-on? And why did JJ Gabriel leave?

The simple answer for many, and we can take the Paraguayan left-back Diego León as our example here, is that they are plainly not good enough and signing them has been poor . Some will take time, Sekou Kone was brought in from Mali and is out on loan at Lausanne to gain experience. Developing footballers is not an exact science and bringing them in from all around the world is a complex process to begin with. It is reliant on human factors outside football, of whether they can quickly adapt to life in a new country before even thinking about what they do on the pitch.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Manchester United have a new head coach. Mauricio Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked after leading the club to their worst start to a season in four decades.

In a tearful farewell to the US men’s national team, Pochettino called the move “one of the most difficult decisions” of his career. But the job he inherits may be harder still. No team in Europe’s top five leagues has conceded more goals in all competitions this season. Bruno Fernandes has rejected a second offer of a new contract. And fans have turned their anger on the hierarchy above the dugout.

In his analysis of what the new head coach must do, Will Unwin wrote that whoever took over would have to find solutions on the pitch while putting pressure on those above him: “United fans know the person in the dugout cannot take all the blame and someone else has to be publicly accountable.”

Pochettino’s first game is at Liverpool on Sunday, then Sporting away in the Champions League. So is he the right man for the job? Can he get a tune out of this squad, and who will thrive under his high-intensity style? And will the club’s owners give him the time and the tools he needs?

Will, who covers Manchester United for the Guardian, will be live here at 2pm GMT on Thursday 19 November to answer your questions.

Post your questions in the comments below or email conversations@theguardian.com

items.title: Black Friday Garmin deals - Big discounts on computers, watches and hardware
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Garmin products are some of the most popular items on sale during the Black Friday sales event.

Garmin bike computers, smartwatches, lights, trainers and other hardware are often discounted, and the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales are often a good time to bag yourself a new piece of tech.

Amazon, Garmin and Sigma Sports in the UK all have a host of discounted Garmin hardware already, with some very good prices for computers and watches.

Let's kick off with the Forerunner 265? Want a quality smartwatch without going crazy on the price? This is it.

Currently at its lowest-ever price, the 265 will cover all of your running needs. You can also use Spotify to take care of your music, as well as just using it as a cool everyday watch. View Deal

The popular Forerunner 970 smartwatch is 13% off in three different colours. This premium running- and triathlon-focused smartwatch is geared to help you run and also provides HRV status and sleep metrics.

This bundle deal from Garmin also comes with a Power Bank included to help with charging when needed.View Deal

The fēnix 8 is 25% off already; this is the cheapest it has ever been on Amazon. There are also five versions to choose from in the 47mm face size variant.

The Edge Explore 3 may have arrived, but the Explore 2 is still available and is a good option for riders prioritising navigation features without a lot of other bells and whistles.

The Edge 540 is 14% off right now, though it was available for $244 last November. This is a good unit for all-around riding; keep watching to see if the price drops a little more. View Deal

The Edge 840 is at its lowest price in 30 days on Amazon right now, though it has been on sale for less cash this year. Officially, this unit has been superceded by the 850, but it's still a very capable unit with a touchscreen. View Deal

The Edge 550 is on sale right now with a healthy 20% off. This is a mighty computer, but we felt the lack of a touchscreen limited it slightly. If you are happy with buttons, take a look.

The Edge 850 is also on sale, discounted by 17%. In essence, this is the 550 with a touchscreen. It's a slightly bigger unit with a touchscreen, a built-in speaker and all the usual Garmin training and fitness tools. View Deal

The Edge 1040 Solar doesn't show a discount on Amazon right now, but it's $50 cheaper from the Garmin Amazon store than it is on their website sale right now, so I'm including the deal for you. If you want some Solar charging tech in a big unit this is a good unit. View Deal

The Garmin Edge 1050 is a top-tier Garmin unit and is arguably still worth buying over the recently launched and more expensive Edge 1060.

$100 off, this unit is a monster, with a brilliant, clear display and fast touchscreen.

This unit pairs a rear light with a Bluetooth radar to help you monitor upcoming vehicles from up to 153 yards away. If you want a built-in camera too, scroll down. View Deal

The Varia RCT715 is on sale in the US at 25% off. This unit brings together a camera, taillight and radar to help keep you safer on the bike. It Bluetooth-pairs with your head unit so you can view radar alerts.

The Garmin Varia Vue is 27% off if you want to invest in front and rear Varia units. This camera/light pairs a 600-lumen front light with a 4K camera to capture your rides. Tip: You will need a Micro SD card for the unit too. View Deal

The Flux 2 is discounted on the Garmin website; it's a solid smart trainer that prioritises low noise and is accurate within 2.5%. The trainer can connect with all the usual indoor training apps, so you can have a solid winter of riding. View Deal

The Tacx Neo 2T with Zwift Cog and Click is 18% off right now. This top-level trainer comes with Zwift's Cog and Click sprocket pre-installed, plus clip-on virtual shifters, so you can use it easily with any bike. It also works without power in standalone mode, which is useful for races, events, or outdoor riding.View Deal

Want to go the whole hog with a premium smart bike? Th Neo Bike Plus has a 10% discount. This is a fully adjustable smart bike that aims to offer the ultimate immersion indoors. The trainer vibrates and simulates road surfaces; dynamic inertia tech makes it feel like an outdoor ride, and the built-in fans mimic wind and keep you cool. View Deal

Garmin's latest RS210 power meter pedals are on sale. This deal is for the RS210 dual-sided SPD SL option which gained recharging capability over the previous units battery powered tech. SPD and SPD-SL pedal bodies can be switched onto the axles, and the pedals are accurate to within +/-1%. View Deal

The Forerunner 55 is a nice entry point into the world of smartwatches and has a healthy discount in the black colour.

This watch will suit runners, but will suit anyone just wanting a Garmin smartwatch with its two-week battery life. View Deal

This early BF deal sees the fēnix 8 drop to its lowest ever price on Amazon in the 47 mm/slate grey version.

The fēnix 8 is a top-level smartwatch with voice control and contactless payment tech. Its AMOLED screen is punchy and vivid, yet you still get up to 29 days of battery life in smartwatch mode. View Deal

The Garmin Varia RCT715 is at 15% on Amazon, the same as Sigma and the Garmin sale.

The RCT715 is a light, camera and rear radar in one and has daylight visibility up to a mile.

The Edge Explore 2 is a more basic unit that prioritises mapping and navigation. It doesn't have as many bells and whistles, but if that's all you need, it's a solid buy.

This is a really good price for the Garmin Edge 540. A solid little computer that's packed with a load of features. It doesn't have a touchscreen, so consider this point if it's a deal-breaker for you.

The Edge 840 unit is just over 20% off and is available for under £300. This is a solid operator, but the Edge 850 which got an upgraded colour touschcreen is also on sale below. View Deal

Here's the solar-charging version of the Edge 840, also on sale with 25% off. If you live somewhere with lots of sunshine, this will be worth a look. I didn't find the solar tech too useful in the UK.

The Garmin Edge 850 is also discounted by just under 20% in the Sigma sale. This unit has a colour touchscreen and has lots of advanced training features.View Deal

This is a big saving on the Edge 1040 Solar, with over 25% off. In bright sunlight, we found it could go weeks without charging. Making it ideal for long rides or touring.

Garmin's flagship model until the recent launch of the 1060, the 1050 is a powerhouse, with a built-in bell and contactless pay technology. It's packed with features; do you need them all?

items.title: Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd
items.content: <article>Culture, defence and Bruno Fernandes - the key issues facing Mauricio Pochettino as he takes over as Manchester United boss.</article>
items.lbText:
"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."

Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.

The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.

The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.

Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.

So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?

"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino

Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.

"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.

Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.

It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.

However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.

Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.

The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.

He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.

For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.

Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a £50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with £70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.

Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.…

items.title: ‘Who is influencing whom and why?’ – Some of cycling’s biggest backers are spinning a sponsorship spiderweb, but what are the risks?
items.author: Chris Marshall-Bell
items.content:
At Spain’s biggest cycling races next year, one sponsor will be ubiquitous: Lidl.

Plastered across the red leader’s jersey at the men’s and women’s Vuelta a España will be the logo of the German supermarket chain; it’ll also adorn barriers and finish gantries at the Volta a Catalunya and the Itzulia Basque Country; and in each and every race, riders from Lidl-Trek, also emblazoned with the discount chain’s red-yellow-blue coat of arms, will be competing. Given the team’s big-spending habits of recent times, it’s not unfeasible that a Lidl rider will win (many) a Lidl race.

The newly announced sponsorship deals – which are in addition to the Lidl Deutschland Tour, and come three years after Lidl was a major sponsor of the 2023 UCI Road World Championships – are another sign of Lidl’s commitment and interest in mass-participation sport; alongside cycling, it has also significantly invested in football and handball. As the company's customer base and profits reach new heights, so too does its marketing strategy. To promote an active lifestyle to its millions of loyal and new customers, it wants to be seen as the supermarket of choice for athletes and active people.

But does Lidl further extending its tentacles into cycling pose a problem? Is there a risk that too much of the same thing risks threatening the sport? To get to the point: is there a possible conflict of interest issue to address?

Lidl is not the only cycling sponsor with fingers in many pies. MyWhoosh, the virtual cycling platform, has been a long-time sponsor of the world’s best team, UAE Team Emirates-XRG, while simultaneously hosting the UCI Esports World Championships. Similarly, MyWhoosh’s rival, Zwift, is the main sponsor of the Tour de France Femmes, while simultaneously sponsoring the Canyon-Sram team.

Elsewhere, French petrochemical giant TotalEnergies had a team competing in the Tour de France this year, while also being a major partner of the race itself. There are other examples: car brand Škoda, as well as bike component manufacturer Shimano, are also linked with numerous different cycling stakeholders. The list runs and runs.

It’s not a situation unique to cycling: similar multi-partnership arrangements are found in other sports, especially football. The UAE-based airline Emirates, for example, sponsors many of Europe’s biggest clubs, as well as the English FA Cup, the world’s oldest competition. Formula One can point to its own examples.

No evidence – let alone suggestion – has ever been raised of private companies interfering with the integrity of cycling competition. But has cycling reached a point where a select number of brands are spreading their wings uncomfortably wide, leaving open the possibility of them potentially having too much influence over the sport?

Power, success, and a particular image

Sponsors have held sway over cycling teams since bike racing began. Bike teams, after all, are funded by external backers, and they wouldn't exist without their support. Companies telling a team it must select X rider for X race for visibility purposes, as much as for competitive reasons, happened at the outset of bike racing in the 19th century and still happens today.

He and his team would say different, of course, but do you really think Tadej Pogačar has ridden the UAE Tour four times (and is expected to make his fifth appearance in 2027) because he views it as better preparation for his main season goals than, say, the more competitive and less sprint-focused Paris-Nice or Tirreno-Adriatico? It’s unlikely, but his appearance also serves the commercial and promotional interests of the team’s principal backers to have its headline rider in its state-supported home race. The story repeats across the cycling landscape: riders and teams make certain decisions based on the wishes, and sometimes demands, of those who provide the funds. There is nothing inherently wrong with that.

In the first quarter of this century, major international sponsors have shifted their marketing approach, favouring cross-promotion with similar but different partners to reach as wide and as diverse an audience as possible. "Companies realised a long time ago that sponsoring an event is not enough, as some have visibility but others don’t," Professor Jean-Loup Chappelet, one of the world’s leading sports governance academics, told .

"Sponsoring an athlete is better. It goes back a long way; look at Adidas and Nike sponsoring runners. They may sponsor an event as well, and there will be signs around the stadium, like there are on the road in cycling races, but the athlete gives them more visibility. As a result, every sponsor now does both: they have a team of athletes and sponsor events."

Professor Simon Chadwick, who is a leading voice on sport’s geopolitics and economics, concurred. "It’s about power and also projecting a particular image: we are successful, and we associate with successful sports teams and events," he said. "Emirates has the money and power associated with many leading football teams [and the UAE men's cycling team – ed], and they’ve successfully established a narrative that it and its associated clubs are the best of everything."

In a statement to , Lidl said of its various, concurrent relationships: "By partnering with various stakeholders… we aim to support the entire cycling ecosystem. This multi-layered commitment allows us to foster equal opportunities, prominently supporting both men’s and women’s cycling, and to bring the sport closer to a broader audience."

But do these spiderweb-like agreements constitute a headache for sports authorities? "Dense, highly interconnected and deeply embedded relationships exist that are increasingly throwing up contradictions and juxtapositions, meaning we get situations where people are asking questions," Chadwick continued.

"There is no doubt that there is evidence [in other sports] of commercial partners and sponsors seeking to, if not directly intervene to achieve outcomes that they are pursuing, then certainly trying to exert influence."

Evidence of sponsors directly impacting the result of cycling competition is in short supply. What appears more likely, and has been demonstrably proven in a wide range of sports, is that sponsors garner influence at a governmental level. That could mean they earn a seat at the table that decides venue selection for a tournament, or have a word in the ear of a committee member voting on regulation changes.

This is particularly relevant with Lidl: in the ongoing battle to reform professional cycling’s economic model and structural issues, understands that a Lidl employee is part of the UCI’s reform working group, while at the same time Lidl has become a shareholder in the team-led venture, Collective Cycling Group (CCG). That means the German company has a stake in both projects, which could give it influence over decisions that will shape the future of the sport projects.

"You can’t separate these things: governance, hierarchy, big networks, big money, the state, private equity investors," Chadwick added. "It’s become such a dense network that it’s difficult to even begin to unravel it or draw red lines."

The possible issues affecting cycling and the weight a small group of sponsors could have over the sport are worth spelling out – even if, it must be said, they are merely hypothetical for this essay, and there is no evidence that such incidents would eventuate.

If a rider is punished due to an in-race incident, could that team’s sponsor, who also has links to the UCI, use its leverage with the governing body to reduce said rider’s sanction? Could a situation also arise in which an event sponsor lobbies a race organiser to tailor a route towards a rider from a team that they also financially back?

Companies might not even need to wield such clout: those in charge of making decisions might be subconsciously swung towards a particular decision, aware of who is paying for the running of the event or the team. That is essentially how soft power works.

"Lidl operates with a strict, structural separation between its commercial marketing partnerships and sporting operations," a spokesperson for the supermarket said. "As a sponsor of race events, our role is strictly commercial – for example, focused on fan engagement and promoting fresh food.

"We have no involvement in, or influence over, race organisation, sporting regulations, or the decisions made by race juries and the UCI. The sporting integrity of the races is exclusively safeguarded by the independent race organisers and the sport’s governing body.

"When Lidl-Trek competes in a race where Lidl acts as a commercial partner, the team is subject to the exact same sporting rules and competitive conditions as every other team. The race organisers and UCI commissaires ensure an entirely neutral competitive environment. There is no structural or operational overlap between Lidl’s race partnership activation and the Lidl-Trek sporting department."

On the Collective Cycling Group, Lidl said discussions to strengthen cycling's long-term sustainability were ongoing and directed us to the UCI for queries relating to its reform working group.

When asked for a comment on the topic, Škoda said: "Škoda Auto has been a long-standing supporter of cycling and works with a range of partners across the sport. Our partnerships are based on clearly defined commercial and sponsorship agreements and do not extend to sorting decisions or competition outcomes. We respect the respective roles and independence of governing bodies, organisers and teams and conduct our partnerships accordingly."

Additionally, MyWhoosh's Director of E-Sports and Game Operations, Matt Smithson, said: "MyWhoosh is proud to invest across cycling, from our long-standing partnership with UAE Team Emirates-XRG to hosting the UCI Cycling Esports World Championships.

"Each of these is a commercial partnership with clearly defined roles. We have no involvement in team selection, results or sporting decisions in racing. These rest with the UCI, race organisers and the teams themselves. At the UCI Cycling Esports World Championships, the competition rules and results are governed by the UCI. We fully respect the UCI's governance framework and the independence of those who run and officiate the sport.

"Our aim is to grow cycling and make it more accessible to riders everywhere."

What's the UCI's stance on it all?

Speaking more broadly about the perceived conflict of interest, Chadwick added: "This gets to the battle for the soul of sport. What type of governance is there? Are there conflicts of interest? Who is influencing whom and why, and how are they doing that?

"Where is the money coming from, and why is it coming from there? What do people want in return, and who is taking what? That raises the fundamental issue of integrity: who makes decisions about rules? Sports fans need to know that rules are being created fairly and equitably, not on the basis of whoever paid to be a commercial partner. This is where we get issues around rules, bribery and corruption.

"In general, sport has made some progress in the past 20 years towards being better governed, more transparent, fairer and more equitable. But the reality is, despite all the deeds and good words, governance in sport is still really opaque."

In a statement to , the UCI said that it has a "clear governance framework to deal with potential conflicts of interest". It said that the "same brand cannot be the main sponsor of two professional teams at the same time", adding that "the principal partners and paying agent… may act in that capacity for one team only." Members of those teams, "which include its sponsors, may have no link with another UCI WorldTour, a UCI ProTeam [equivalent provisions apply to women’s teams] or the organiser of a UCI WorldTour event that is likely to influence the sporting course of events, or to be perceived as doing so."

There are examples in cycling of a sponsor’s logo being emblazoned on different kits: TotalEnergies on its eponymous team’s and Netcompany-Ineos’s; Red Bull, meanwhile, owns Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe and is on the sleeve of Tudor Pro Cycling’s jersey. There is no suggestion that either sponsor has sought to favour one team or another in competition.

"When a company chooses to acquire sponsorship rights in several areas of cycling, whether teams, events or the UCI itself, this is a commercial decision based on the visibility each partnership brings to its brand. These rules are designed precisely to strike the right balance: allowing our sport to benefit from this investment while safeguarding the integrity of sporting results."

The responsibility to scrutinise potential problems lies with the UCI Ethics Commission, an independent body that reports its annual findings at each year’s UCI congress.

Biting the hand that feeds you

As the UCI alluded to, mid-sized sports like cycling that are dependent on sponsorship revenue just to survive, let alone thrive, cannot be too picky with where the capital that bankrolls athletes, teams, races and federations is coming from. "One of the core elements in this is the feeling that if we don’t agree terms with them [a partner] then they’ll go somewhere else," Chadwick said.

FOMO – fear of missing out – is real. "Of course it is," Chadwick adds. "But it’s not about a rival team or their riders, but a rival sport. You could sponsor cycling, but you could sponsor golf or tennis instead. Whoever secures that big money will secure a competitive advantage. It’s a common story across many sports."

The consequence of that is that it creates an uneasy situation in which the very questions being mused in this article are asked. "What always talks loudest in sport are not the governing bodies, athletes or fans – it’s the money," Chadwick said. "I remember once being with the sponsorship team of one European governing body, and I asked them on what basis they signed deals with partners. Was it an alignment with values, a particular target market, I asked. ‘No’, they said, ‘there's one criteria only – who pays the most’."

Ultimately, that gives further weight to the sponsors: they know that cycling teams and events are desperate for money, and thus often can’t risk an argument with their paymasters.

Yet perhaps this is all simply a case of making a mountain out of a molehill. Chappelet, who has spent decades researching sports governance, particularly in Olympic circles, suspects it might be. "I do not see a conflict of interest between sponsoring a cyclist and a UCI-sanctioned race organiser, or the UCI itself," he said.

History would agree with Chappelet. As previously noted, there is zero evidence of companies using their leverage to swing a decision towards their supported entity; it bears repeating, none of the hypothetical scenarios mentioned in this article (interfering in disciplinary decisions, venue announcements and course design) have ever been recorded, and nor is there any indication that such companies would look to flex their muscles in this regard.

And there’s another point worth addressing: if a sponsor like Lidl or MyWhoosh cut off its funding to cycling, would the teams or races it sponsors even survive? It’s not a guarantee that a replacement sponsor would step up. Don't bite the hand that feeds you, one might caution.

But as long as a select few sponsors continue writing cheques for riders, teams and the sport’s governing body, the uncomfortable, hard-to-breach matter of undue influence will persist in the background. Even with UCI frameworks that are designed to require transparent governance safeguards – and which, on the face of it, do just that – the reality is that part of cycling’s integrity is dependent on trusting in corporate financiers to act morally and ethically for the benefit of the sport and not for their own commercial interests.

items.title: NSN Cycling Team change bikes for the second time in three seasons as German brand returns to the WorldTour
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
NSN Cycling Team will ride Cube bikes for the 2027 season and beyond after the team struck a deal with the German manufacturer.

Cube will provide the outfit’s World and Development teams with their Litening C:68X Aero and Air road bikes, while the Aerium C:68X will be deployed for time trials. The bikes will roll on Newmen’s Streem range of wheels, with SRAM providing the group sets and other components, while the saddles will be provided by Selle Italia.

Cube will be the team’s third bike partner in as many seasons. Factor provided their rides for a number of seasons when the squad were known as Israel-Premier Tech, but moved on at the end of the 2025 season, with Scott bikes taking their place for the 2026 season.

Now, with the arrival of high-profile GC riders, Primož Roglič and Richard Carapaz for the 2027 season, the team will be hoping for some stability, though it is a return to the familiar for their star sprinter, Biniam Girmay, who rode the brand’s bikes at Wanty-intermarché.

"We are incredibly excited to welcome Cube as our Official Bike Partner," said NSN’s General Manager, Kjell Carlström.

"From our first conversations, it was clear that we share the same vision and ambition. Cube's passion for innovation and commitment to performance make them an ideal partner for our team, as we continue to grow.

"In 2027, we will have more of a General Classification focus and the support from Cube will be fundamental to our success across the entire racing calendar.

"Of course, Biniam Girmay won three Tour de France stages and the green jersey with Cube, so we are looking forward to seeing Bini and his teammates create more memories."

Based in Bavaria, Cube were most recently in the WorldTour in 2025, providing bikes for Intermarché-Wanty, but when that team merged with Lotto for last season, they were forced out in favour of the Flemish squad’s Orbea bikes.

"From our first conversations through to the work already underway, we have been impressed by the team’s professionalism and its clear focus on performance," Cube’s founder and owner, Marcus Pürner, said.

"The team’s ambitions, reflected in its impressive new signings, such as Richard Carapaz and Kasper Asgreen and latest addition Primož Roglič, align closely with our own plans and long-term strategy.

"For us, this partnership also offers a valuable opportunity to work closely with the riders and technical staff, using their feedback and experience to support the continued development of our bikes."

items.title: Game Preview: Knicks at Timberwolves, November 19, 2026
