items.lbText:
New head coach faces tough opening match at Anfield

‘It’s a big challenge but at the same time it’s adrenaline’

Mauricio Pochettino said it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the new Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.

Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff landed earlier in the week to begin work at Carrington , laying the foundations as United seek to turn their season around. His right-hand man, Jesús Pérez, the goalkeeping coach Toni Jiménez and the fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino, who continues to work with his father, have already taken training with those not on international duty.

Those away with their national teams will return to the club on Thursday, when they are expected to meet Pochettino for the first time and hold meetings. Conversations have also been held with various departments within the club, as Pochettino sought to learn about the squad’s health as he seeks areas of improvement.

Pochettino’s first challenge will be at Anfield on Sunday, when 18th-placed United take on Liverpool. The 54-year-old has his eyes set on rattling Manchester City after being told on TNT Sports that “Manchester’s blue and always will be blue” by DaMarcus Beasley, who once had a loan spell with City. Pochettino responded: “No way. You will see. Give me time … give me time and that is going to start to change.”

Speaking about joining United, Pochettino said: “It’s a big challenge but at the same time, it’s adrenaline that you want to feel because I think we are going to have a different job. But I think one of the things that is important is that we have the experience to deal with that, and I think we need to add our common sense and the way we are going to approach all the things.

“We know that the situation is not a situation that a club like Manchester United deserves,” Pochettino added. “The fanbase is amazing and after we signed here in America, of every 10 people I crossed in the street, nine are Manchester United fans. It’s amazing.”

Pochettino is also reunited with the strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya, the analyst Alec Scott and his long-term assistant, Miki D’Agostino, at Old Trafford.

items.title: 24 Top Cycling Teams Are Making A New Money Move To Fix Cycling’s Business Model
items.author: ahood
items.content: Two dozen teams join forces in a new venture to try to create untapped revenue streams to help underwrite today's super team budgets. Can they fix cycling's business model?
items.lbText:
Teams are floating a new project to collectively sell what they bring to the peloton. (Photo: Loic VENANCE / AFP via Getty Images)

Top pro teams are taking another stab at trying to fix cycling’s business model.

Some 24 squads are forming a company designed to turn their collective commercial muscle into new revenue steams.

Collective Cycling Group Ltd. (CCG), a UK-based business owned by participating teams, announced a shareholder agreement including teams from the men’s and women’s WorldTour and ProTeam ranks.

Discussions with additional teams are ongoing, a statement confirmed Wednesday.

“Teams carry much of the sporting and financial risk in professional cycling, while many of the sport’s commercial opportunities remain fragmented,” CCG director Oliver Ciesla said in the announcement. “The UCI reform process creates a first opportunity to address these challenges together.”

Instead of making a run directly at TV rights, which are controlled by races, teams are looking at what they bring to the table in the form of cycling’s biggest stars.

The idea is to bundle what they have into something bigger that fans, broadcasters, and sponsors might be interested in paying money for.

That includes team commercial rights, data, media content, merchandising, hospitality, and fan experiences.

The end game is to give teams a stronger financial footing rather than leaving them constantly chasing the next sponsor and relying almost exclusively on sponsorship backing to underwrite ever-rising team budgets.

The announcement follows the stalled ONE Cycling project , which died on the vine after the UCI rejected it in June 2025 .

Corporate filings show CCG previously operated under the name OneCycling Limited, according to Reuters .

The release doesn’t mention a new racing series or a call for shared broadcast revenues.

Instead, the focus is on developing commercial opportunities around assets the teams already hold.

They hope to organize their newest project as part of the UCI’s ongoing Project 2030 effort to reshape professional road cycling.

The announcement does not identify the 24 teams, disclose financial commitments, or set a timetable for its first products.

Cycling’s tried this before. Let’s see if something will change.

items.title: Testing the Tech and Heat Training Required to Survive a 95-Degree Tour de France
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: From Q36.5 cooling apparel to physiological heat blocks, we stepped into a climate chamber to find out what it really takes to combat extreme temperatures.
items.lbText:
There is a giant vault in Bolzano, Italy that can simulate elevation higher than Mount Everest, a freeze as cold as Siberia, and temperatures so hot that they are used to help train firefighters. On October 21, I stepped into that vault wearing nothing but a cycling kit and shoes.

As I swung my leg over a stationary bike, the fans revved up in front of me as the chamber adjusted its climate to match Stage 2 of this year’s Tour de France. It was a hot day in Barcelona when Isaac del Toro won ahead of Tadej Pogacar and Remco Evenepoel. By the end of the Tour, it was the hottest race on record with an average temperature of 32.4°C (90.3°F) across the 21 stages.

Excessive heat usually means a decline in performance. But with the advent of heat training, cooling strategies, and ever-improving clothing technology, professional cyclists are faster than ever, even during the hottest Tour de France in history.

The moment I stepped into the vault — the TerraX Cube — I knew what was at stake. I was here alongside the CORE team and more than 20 other journalists to test the new Q36.5 Gregarius Pro Evo Jersey, Base Layer Subzero, and Dottore Pro Bib Shorts. The vault was set to 35°C (95°F) degrees with a humidity of 50%, far from the ideal temperature to achieve peak performance. I had just done a heat training session in CORE’s Sweatlab, so I had a baseline of data for what I could expect as my core temperature rose.

Not only were we going to ride in excessive heat, we were going to simulate the finale of Stage 2 of the Tour using a custom workout on Zwift. Here was the workout , along with my power targets based on my FTP:

I was already dripping sweat during the warmup thanks to the ambient temperature, and my sweat rate intensified as my power increased to 360w. After a quick recovery, we began the hardest part of the test (in my opinion): four minutes at VO2 Max in 95-degree heat. This is the type of effort short enough that you can maintain an output above threshold, but long enough that your heart rate and RPE will be jacked up by the end of the effort.

The final few intervals went by fast as I could see the metaphorical finish line in front of me. And just like that, it was all over. CORE gathered data from our body temperature sensors, and we shuffled our way into the cool hallway. The testing was over; now it was time to look at the results.

To my surprise, our performances in the heat chamber didn’t drop off significantly. In fact, many riders (myself included) performed at their best despite the hot conditions. This was a sharp contrast to my data from CORE’s Sweatlab where I pushed myself to the limit without ever breaking 300w.

The lab test at CORE – done two days before the test in Bolzano – was a data-gathering mission. I wasn’t there to chase power PBs or set an impressive time. I was there to sweat; and that I did.

During the normal cooling conditions, I wore a cycling kit and had two fans pointed towards me. I was riding on a Zwift Ride with ERG mode turned on, so my power output was steady to the Watt. The initial 15-minute interval established the baseline where my heart rate was steady at 138 bpm, and my core temperature stabilized at 38°C (100.4°F).

The hard part was up next: 35 minutes of heat training. That meant pulling on the CORE heat training suit, turning the fans off, and turning the heater on. Within minutes, my sweat started pooling on the floor. Over the course of 35 minutes, my heart rate rose from 138 bpm to 175 bpm without any change in power. I rode at 280w the entire time, but it felt like I was doing a threshold interval for the last 15 minutes.

That is the damage that heat can do to your performance. Without sufficient cooling, Zone 2 power can feel like Zone 4 power once your heat strain reaches a certain level. That was the kind of performance degradation that CORE was looking for in the Italian climate cube. But the closer they looked at the results, the more they realized that the clothing had worked.

We were all wearing Q36.5 kit in the climate chamber, specifically designed for use in 30°C+ (86°F) heat. Tom Pidcock loves heat training, and it was no surprise to hear that he plays a major role in the R&D of Q36.5 kit. (Fun fact: he’s also the only rider on Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team who wears an XXS skinsuit.)

As I pored through my own performance data, I remembered how good my legs felt during the final two-minute interval in the heat chamber. Despite feeling hot, my body had performed extremely well in the conditions. Personally, that is the biggest difference that I’ve noticed after doing a heat training block.

Without heat acclimatization, my body has typically reacted to the heat like it did in CORE’s Sweatlab. My heart rate would rise uncontrollably as my legs are drained of their strength. But after a big heat training block, I noticed that I could still hit my best power numbers in excessively hot conditions. Not only would my heart rate be 10 bpm lower than expected, but it would stabilize during long efforts in the heat – quite the opposite of what I experienced in the CORE Sweatlab.

One of my biggest takeaways was that the clothing had worked. This wasn’t the only heat adaptation method that I asked Q36.5 and CORE about during this trip. I also asked about cold drinks, pouring water over your head, rubbing ice cubes on your wrists, and of course, heat training. Let’s start with what does work.

Cold drinks and gels are probably the most effective ways to cool your body from the inside out. When you’re talking about performance degradation in the heat, you are most often talking about an increase in core temperature as well as an increase in skin temperature. This is known as heat strain, something that CORE quantifies with their sensor and app, and the key metric that many riders use for heat training.…

items.title: Primož Roglič Lands a Contract to Join NSN Cycling for 2027
items.author: ahood
items.content: Roglič signs late-hour deal with NSN Cycling for 2027 that will keep the popular Slovenian in the WorldTour for at least one more season.
items.lbText:
Roglič joins NSN on a one-year deal. (Photo: Marco BERTORELLO / AFP via Getty Images)

Primož Roglič will race in 2027 and will join NSN Cycling on a one-year deal.

In a late-hour move, the deal means the 37-year-old Slovenian will be in the WorldTour peloton next season.

“I always like challenges,” Roglič said in a team note. “That’s why I’m here, to take these on together and see what the future brings us.

“It took me some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never. It feels like the perfect connection.”

Roglič, one of the superstars over the past decade, was looking down the barrel at possible retirement at the end of 2026.

Talks with several teams ended without a signature , but things came together quickly with NSN Cycling.

“From the first moment we spoke, it was evident that Primož still has a lot of passion for the sport and a drive to be the best he can,” said NSN Cycling general manager Kjell Carlström. “It was an easy decision to make.”

The former ski jumper ended his three-year run with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after a season that included second overall at the Vuelta a España and a win at the European time trial championship.

It was more of a question if he wanted to keep racing and at what price.

Roglič was sometimes bizarrely ambivalent in his public statements about his future, but he was talking with several teams behind the scenes.

Talks petered out, however, with one team after another. NSN offered a one-year contract but no financial details were revealed.

Roglič was reportedly earning around $3 million a year with Red Bull, so a high asking price might have been a factor on some teams taking a pass on the veteran.

Roglič — a winner of five grand tours — will link up with Richard Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt on the reinvigorated NSN lineup.

“This signing reflects the ambition we have for the future. We want to compete at the highest level, challenge for major results and continue building a team capable of achieving great things,” Carlström said. “We are confident that Primož can play an important role in that journey, and we look forward to seeing him race in NSN colors.”

Roglič scored nearly 1,000 UCI points in 2026 , something that will come in handy if he can repeat it next season for NSN Cycling.

The team — formerly Israel-Premier Tech — finished ranked 19th in the rolling three-year WorldTour rankings, one spot out of the guaranteed top 18 licenses.

There’s no news yet on a possible calendar, but at NSN he should see plenty of chances to race.

“I still believe I have some work to do, in both racing and with myself,” Roglič said. “I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things.”

The team broke the news on social media, with a smiling Roglič using a “like and follow” of the team’s social media channel.

Roglič — who was beaten by Tadej Pogačar at the wild TT finale at the 2020 Tour de France — will join his new teammates at a winter camp in Spain next month.

items.title: Primož Roglič will continue racing into 2027 as new team for 'final chapter' is finally revealed
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
After months of speculation, Primož Roglič will continue his career into 2027, having signed with NSN Cycling Team on a one-year contract.

The 37-year-old looked to be heading for retirement after his time with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe came to an end – despite being the reigning European time trial champion and having finished second at the Vuelta a España in September – but with NSN, he has found a place for the final chapter of his storied career.

A five-time Grand Tour winner, Roglič will make up part of the Swiss WorldTour team’s general classification ambitions, alongside fellow new signings for 2027, Richard Carapaz and Lennert Van Eetvelt.

"I always like challenges. That's why I'm here, to take these on together and see what the future brings us," said Roglič on the team's website.

"It took me some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never. It feels like the perfect connection.

"I still believe I have some work to do – in both racing and with myself. I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things."

10 years after his first WorldTour season with LottoNL-Jumbo, former ski jumper Roglič will arrive at NSN as the rider with the most victories among active men's pros at 93, only trailing Slovenian compatriot Tadej Pogačar.

Now into his late 30s, he's raced limited calendars in recent seasons, but can still ramp up his performance for the big occasion at Grand Tours, finishing second at the most recent Vuelta, eighth at last year's Tour de France, and winning his fourth Vuelta title as recently as 2024.

Delighted by bringing in the talents of one of the modern era's best GC riders, NSN revealed their new star signing with a social media post of Roglič following NSN on Instagram.

"Welcoming Primož Roglič to NSN Cycling Team is a hugely exciting moment for our organization. From the first moment we spoke, it was evident that Primož still has a lot of passion for the sport and a drive to be the best he can. It was an easy decision to make," said NSN General Manager Kjell Carlström.

"Primož is one of the outstanding riders of his generation. His achievements speak for themselves, and the opportunity to bring someone with his experience, quality and winning mentality into our team is something we are incredibly proud of.

"This signing reflects the ambition we have for the future. We want to compete at the highest level, challenge for major results and continue building a team capable of achieving great things. We are confident that Primož can play an important role in that journey, and we look forward to seeing him race in NSN colours."

items.author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
items.content:

In a theater high up in a midtown Manhattan skyscraper built from lots of glass, a highlight reel played to deafening music. And then, on “a monumental day for US Soccer”, federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, announced they had bagged their man, Mauricio Pochettino, to become the highest-profile United States manager in the men’s national team’s history.

items.lbText:
The incoming Manchester United manager improved the US team’s culture and competitiveness, but could not bring about sea change in two years

I n a theater high up in a midtown Manhattan skyscraper built from lots of glass, a highlight reel played to deafening music. And then, on “a monumental day for US Soccer”, federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, announced they had bagged their man, Mauricio Pochettino , to become the highest-profile United States manager in the men’s national team’s history.

Pochettino held court for three-quarters of an hour in his signature blend of Spanglish before the assembled media and a grab bag of sponsors. Then he recorded some TV hits. And after that, in a bit of accidental prescience, he went off to record a podcast with Gary Neville.

Two years, two months, and a week later, he presided over the USMNT’s untroubled 2-0 win over Haiti in Cincinnati on Tuesday, putting a bow on an 8-0 aggregate victory in the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals. He did a lot of hugging afterwards, a staple of what was briefly mooted as Pochismo . He posed for a group picture with federation staffers. There were tears in the locker room.

After a 6-0 romp in the first leg on Saturday, Pochettino left his starting XI unchanged, raising some eyebrows. Perhaps he hoped to leave with another emphatic result; maybe he was buffing up his final stats in charge of the USA; or possibly he was legitimately concerned about giving away a lead of half a dozen goals.

It will probably be the last time in quite a long while that Pochettino enjoys a pair of consecutive lopsided victories. He boarded a private jet after the game to take over Manchester United just as soon it landed in England in the morning, leaving a situation where he enjoyed a bank vault’s worth of credit for one where his every result will be dissected and scrutinized for his viability in the job.

For all the hype, for the $6m annual salary – about double what the previous record earner at the federation, Jürgen Klinsmann, had made – and for all the talk of belief and culture and fight, what did Pochettino actually leave behind for his successor to build on? He was impactful, certainly, turning around a moody and slumping generation ambling into a home World Cup bereft of momentum or much discernible enthusiasm. The Argentinian roused the ballyhooed golden generation for four-fifths of a very strong World Cup, turning in displays more convincing and dominant than the program has ever managed on that stage – until it all came undone against Belgium in the last 16.

His time in charge was notable, absolutely. Pochettino got, and brought, lots of attention to the team, although it’s hard to say whether a more workaday manager might not have ridden that same World Cup wave, as the voice of the co-hosts.

Pochettino wasn’t the first USMNT manager to try to play more expansively, more technically, in a more aesthetically pleasing way. Klinsmann tried it, and Gregg Berhalter tried it, too. But Klinsmann didn’t have the players, and Berhalter’s weren’t ready for it. Pochettino did and they were, at long last, and he introduced a tactical sophistication, with deft attacking patterns that regularly unlocked useful spaces.

He also wasn’t the first USMNT manager to fixate on culture and give young talent a chance. But through his selections and his messaging, he reinstated an internal competition for playing time that had seeped away under several consecutive and at times complacent administrations. And he deepened the player pool considerably. Perhaps any old head coach would have spotted the glut of gifted teenagers pushing through and had the wherewithal to bring them along, but Pochettino deserves credit for leaning on the young players, handing them meaningful minutes and responsibility.

While Pochettino leaves the USMNT better than he found them, his spell in charge was not transformational. He brought the Americans no further at a World Cup than they had been before. His statistics – victories in 62% of his matches; 2.08 goals scored per game; 1.29 conceded – are more or less in line with the numbers put up by his permanent predecessors. He did not win the Concacaf Gold Cup or the Nations League when he was occasioned to.

Nor did he take the US to their first World Cup in four decades, as Bob Gansler did in 1990. Or make them respectable on that stage, as Bora Milutinovic did in 1994. Or bring about their breakthrough, as Bruce Arena did in 2002. Or rebuild the program from its modern nadir, as Berhalter did in his first tenure. It is a sign of growth, perhaps, that the strides available to be made were smaller. You can only overcome the challenges you are faced with, after all.

Whatever the case, Pochettino will be remembered fondly by most. He smiled and joked a lot and did his best to say interesting things. He could be spiky , from time to time, but mostly injected an environment that had grown stale and dour with joy.

Pochettino, by all accounts, had a good time stateside, commuting here from his homes in London and Barcelona. He enjoyed watching NFL games and attended the Cincinnati Bengals’ home victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday. He got into country music, apparently. “Only we can say thank you,” Pochettino said in his final news conference, on behalf of his staff. “Thank you so much, and always we are going to keep the good memories.”

The USMNT, too, largely enjoyed their time with their famous coach. They made some nice memories together. But he may not have been here long enough to fundamentally change their trajectory.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now . He teaches at Marist University.

items.title: Broken frame no problem for Lukas Malezsewski, who wins UCI Gravel race after being hit by a driver
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
A broken chainstay proved no problem for Belgian gravel racer Lukas Malezsewski, who won the Greek round of the UCI Gravel World Series last weekend.

Riding for Greg van Avermaet’s GVA Gold team, Malezsewski was just 17km into The Gravel of Marathon race when the incident happened: a driver hit him, breaking the chainstay on the drive side of his Basso bike frame.

But rather than give up, the 25-year-old remounted and raced on, eventually winning the Elite Men’s race more than three minutes ahead of second-placed Kasper Enstad.

In its first edition, The Gravel of Marathon is the first UCI round of the UCI Gravel World Series to be staged in Greece, starting and finishing in the ancient city of Marathon. The Elite men raced over a 95km course, which, though relatively short, comprised more than 1,300m of vertical ascent, with 71% of the course off-road.

Malezsewski was hit by the vehicle after the day’s first climb, and not long after emerging from the route’s second gravel sector. "Got hit by a car after 17km and broke my frame. Still made it to the finish line in first place," Malezsewski wrote in an Instagram post.

Rather than treading the well-worn path to gravel from road racing, Malezsewski is an accomplished mountain bike rider, winning the European junior title in 2019 and the Belgian under-23 title in 2022, though he’s not raced at UCI level since 2024.

While he’s raced occasionally at national and UCI .2 level on the road since then, he’s concentrated on gravel.

And to great effect, winning two UCI races last year and repeating the feat this season, when he won Tartu Rattmaraton in Estonia in mid-September, before finishing in the top six of every other race he started before last weekend’s Greek event.

items.title: 'Tour de France Femmes goal for 2029' – There’s a new US team on the scene, and they have big ambitions
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
The paperwork has been submitted to the UCI and Dr. Andrea Cyr expects to lead the next US-based Continental women's team, Orange Seal presented by Autowurks, in 2027.

The team will be based in Austin, Texas with a "clear ambition" to become a top-25 team in the world with a majority of riders from the United States, and to earn a place in the Tour de France Femmes by 2029.

"We have high aspirations, but the first step is we're going to be a Continental team for 2027. We want to be a ProTeam in 2028, that's where you start to get a lot of the invites like the Classics and bigger UCI stage racing. Then we have a Tour to France Femmes goal of 2029," Cyr told .

"A lot of this is sparked by my own ambition too. There's some development programmes to get people interested in the sport and then there's WorldTour, but there's nothing in between. I'm in a unique position, with resources and networking to actually put things together. A year ago this was not the plan."

The new team merges Cyr's HigherDOSE-Renova criterium-based programme with the former ROXO Continental women's squad, which last competed in 2024 as Boneshaker Project presented by Orange Seal.

"We didn't want this to just be a one-year adventure. We wanted to do something a little bit more sustainable," Cyr said about the next step after HigherDOSE. "So we started conversations with a management group from Texas. All three of these guys have different roles, they've known each other for like 20 years. I think they have found new vigor and motivation through this too."

Leadership at Orange Seal p/b Autowurks includes former WorldTour rider Chann McRae as head sports director, Austin attorney Todd Reed as team manager, and real estate executive Charlie Tames as co-owner. The trio had most recently been involved in supporting French women's ProTeam Mayenne Monbana My Pie. Justin Kirk will split time as a sports director with the women's team and the Texas Roadhouse elite masters team. This quartet of management, along with Cyr, form the ownership group for the team.

"Our goal is to build a top-25 team in the world with a majority of riders from the United States and the resources to compete in the biggest races. Bringing these programs together gives us an established foundation to build on," Tames said in a team statement after a formal launch party in Austin on November 15.

"The 2027 season is the first step toward our top-25 ambition and our goal of reaching the Tour de France Femmes by 2029."

More than half of the roster will come from HigherDOSE, including Cyr and Seitz, with Marjie Bemis, Elizabeth Dixon and Odette Lynch preserving the foundation created in 2026. The ROXO connection brings Femenina a Guatemala stage winner Kira Payer, as well as additional leadership and resources to support the next stage of growth.

Other new riders include Canadian Jenna Nestman, former Fount Cycling rider Alia Shafi, and Nicole Steinmetz, who previously raced for Cynisca and Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY24. According to Cyr, two more riders have been offered contracts and the full roster will be confirmed in the coming weeks.

"American racers are struggling, and it's really struggling on the women's side. I personally started shifting my own goals and my own thinking, and I had a really good result at Pro Road Nationals, a top 10 in the road race, fourth in the crit, and then had a really good result at Philly. I got to thinking, maybe I'm more than just a crit racer," Cyr described to her inspiration to form a new team.

"It was really awesome to have Philly back, and I finished that race [top 15 - Ed.], and I was like, 'That was the best day ever! Like that was my favorite ever.'

"We need more of this, like hard racing with strong teams and strong riders from all over the world. This is what I'm craving, and I know I'm not alone in that. I know a lot of other female racers are probably looking for the same thing."

Once Continental status is confirmed, the team plans to firm the 2027 calendar with UCI races in South America and Europe for the spring, and a return block of racing to Europe in July and August. Key US races will include Redlands Bicycle Classic, Tour of the Gila, USPro Road Nationals and Philadelphia Cycling Classic p/b AmeriGas, as well as a selection of criteriums.

"We want a well-rounded race calendar, but also aware of our short and long-term goals. To achieve our long-term goals, we need to get points and really establish quickly as a strong, confident team," Cyr said.

"It's important to stay engaged with the racing we have here in the U.S., which is a lot of criterium racing. It's good for sponsors."

Orange Seal joins as title sponsor, with Autowurks as presenting sponsor. The team is also supported by bike sponsor Winspace with equipment and apparel partners ABUS, Tifosi, MUMU and Schwalbe.

items.title: Netcompany Ineos lose significant sponsor as TotalEnergies confirms it will not continue in 2027
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
With TotalEnergies moving its financial resources away from the eponymous French ProTeam – which will become XEFI in 2027 – and over to one of the leading women's teams, there were question marks over the company's relationship with the Ineos team.

And now a spokesperson has confirmed to that the sponsorship will not continue beyond this season.

"At the conclusion of these two seasons of sponsorship, TotalEnergies would like to thank the Netcompany INEOS team for its commitment and professionalism, as well as all of its riders, who kept us inspired and excited through their sporting achivements," read a statement.

The news will raise new questions over the finances of Netcompany Ineos, especially in light of the ongoing reports of financial headaches at Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos empire, and the general move towards dilution of its sporting projects.

The company gave up its sole title sponsor’s slot at the cycling team this year, as the Danish IT firm Netcompany was welcomed as a major new backer on a five-year deal.

However, Netcompany’s arrival was not the end of the story, with Tom Hill, the team’s chief commercial officer, saying soon after: “We’re going back to market looking for a second co-title partner.”

There were widespread reports since its arrival at the team in 2025 that TotalEnergies were exploring options for escalation of its sponsorship, including here on where we reported earlier this year that co-title sponsorship was under discussion.

The French energy giant had been clear that it would end its 10-year title backing of Jean-René Bernaudeau’s French team at the end of this season, but clearly wanted to stay in cycling elsewhere.

However, the idea of furthering of the Ineos partnership has broken down at some point and the energy company has gone down a different road, throwing its weight into women’s cycling and the French team that’s home to the world’s top rider, Demi Vollering.

It was interesting that the FDJ team’s manager, Stephen Delcourt, told Cyclingnews that the deal with TotalEnergies came together “very, very fast”, with contact first initiated around the Tour de France Femmes and tied up in a ground-breaking five year deal only a matter of weeks afterwards.

Today’s statement confirms that all its eggs are now in that basket, which raises interesting questions surrounding value for money in terms of the amounts required for the various sponsorship tiers comparing men’s and women’s cycling.

As for Netcompany Ineos, there are no serious doubts surrounding their future after Netcompany’s long-term commitment earlier this year, but the breakdown in the TotalEnergies relationship raises question marks, over how the team will reach the sort of funding levels that the team themselves have acknowledged are required to return to super-team status.

items.title: Hunt Limitless 40 Gravel Aero wheelset review: Good to a fault
items.author: andy@atpperformance.uk (Andy Turner)
items.content:
£1,479.00 / $1,849 / €1,849

1431g claimed,1478g measured with lock rings and tape

40mm front 41mm rear

36mm ext 27mm int Front, 35mm ext 26mm int Rear

With this wheelset, Hunt has applied its Limitless aero technology from the road to gravel, and given my impressions from riding them, it has achieved its goal of making a highly versatile gravel race wheelset to match the latest gravel race frames.

The weight is competitive against some of the best at this depth, making it an impressively good value wheelset. So much so, in fact, that I see no good reason to go for the UD spoke and Ceramic Speed bearing upgrade of this wheelset for another £1000.

But there is the question of tyre width optimisation. Gravel is fast evolving, but current trends are towards wider and wider tyre offerings, with 50mm+ being common across modern races and frame design. These rims are perfect for 40-45mm offerings, but perhaps missing out when it comes to fitting the larger widths that are more prevalent now across races and adventure riding.

Hunt has since released its 5AM Gravel wheelset to cater to that market. They recently tested very well in our wind tunnel gravel wheel shootout, and a review of those will follow in due course.

Design and specifications

These wheels have been designed for racing; At launch, Hunt explicitly stated that this rim shape was designed to be its fastest and most versatile gravel wheelset.

This was done via a combination of CFD (computational fluid dynamics) and wind tunnel development, but also with rider input from sponsored racers. The argument was that modern gravel racing is now mirroring the speed and tactics of road racing. I’d argue that given the speeds of the two, and tactics are very race dependent, but there’s no doubt gravel racing is faster every year.

These Limitless 40 rims have been specifically designed to be optimised with the 40 and 45mm Schwalbe G-One gravel tyres. Testing, which is published on the Hunt website, shows that the Limitless 40 rims were fastest bar the 3T Dicuss 45/50, but those came in at over 300g heavier.

The reason for differing rim profile was due to finding that the air interacts differently with the front and rear wheels, and a wider front and narrower rear was optimal for aero and stability. It’s not an uncommon theme in wheels both on the road and off.

Meanwhile this Limitless technology results in a more squared off rim profile, similar to the latest Roval Terra CLX Aero wheels. This aims to be stable in crosswinds, lighter, and result in a longer virtual aerofoil by cutting the V shape that would be present on a deeper rim, but the idea is that the air continues to flow as if this V is present and elongated, thus ideally resulting in greater aero performance at a shallower depth.

The rim itself is made of unidirectional T24/30 carbon fibre with 3K weave re-enforced spoke holes. Hookless TSS profile is used, with a 4.5mm thick bead to reduce the chance of pinch flats and make the rims stronger in case of a rim strike. Although 40-45mm tyres are recommended, the wheels are safe to use with 35-60mm options.

Spokes are Pillar Wing 20 Elliptical Aero Stainless Steel, with 24 front and rear in a two-cross 1:1 ratio lacing pattern. Dual full-contact sealed cartridge bearings are used with a proprietary waterproof grease used to improve longevity and assist in smooth running across foul weather use. The 48t ratchet drive system at the rear offers fast engagement for accelerations.

Spare spokes are also included with the wheels, along with valves and lockrings, which is not always a given with wheelsets. Proper wheel bags are also included.

First things first, the fitting of tyres. With rims becoming wider and wider, I personally find that tends to mean tyres are more of a pain to fit, with levers being required alongside the elbow grease and trusty grippy gloves. Fitting the Panaracer Gravel King ZX 45mm tyres I’ve been using for all my gravel wheel tests, they were no harder or easier to fit on these rims than similar options.

These are however my first foray into hookless gravel rims. I don’t like hookless for road, mainly because I’m a taller and larger rider, so pressures under 70 PSI feel far too cushioned and squishy for me and make fast cornering unpleasant and the bike feel disconnected.

For gravel, however, this changes. These rims have a max pressure of 58 PSI, which is more than I would use on the tarmac with 45mm tyres, let alone off-road where 30 is around the max pressure I’d run. In this scenario, I am liking hookless quite a lot. It makes leveraging a tyre hook under the bead easy for stubborn removals and promises to reduce manufacturing costs while cutting weight. The super wide rim bead should also be nicely sturdy in the event of a stone strike, but I have not sought those out intentionally.

Weight is an area where these wheels perform pretty well. For the price and depth, 1478g (heavier than claimed but includes lock rings) is fairly lightweight. It’s just over 100g heavier than the UD carbon spoked equipped variant, but that wheelset is the same rim for £1000 more, with ceramic bearings as well. For accelerations I’ve found them responsive, and slow speed climbing does not feel laborious.

Another component that impacts the rapid acceleration is the 48 tooth engagement ratchet. Often these are 36t, which means a 10° engagement, while 48t offers a 7.5° response, so the hub engages after a lesser percentage of the pedal stroke. Some claim that more teeth can reduce longevity, but I’ve yet to have a problem with that.

The rim itself feels nicely stiff, without being excessively so for gravel use. It’s a truncated profile, like the new Roval Terra Aero squared off rim. Spoke lacing wise, the 1:1 two-cross 24 straight pull spoke pattern isn’t anything special on paper, but the wheel feels well balanced without any lag in response when accelerating, while there isn’t any ‘flop’ when banking over.

I have been getting a few spoke pinging noises on rides though, and have yet to be able to determine the cause, but the wheels run true and without issue.

A big component of the performance of this wheelset does depend on what side of the fence you sit on when it comes to tyre widths. I’ve tested everything from 38mm up to 55mm tyres for gravel, and there are pros and cons to each.

We’ve gone through aero testing of gravel tyres, but this metric is very dependent on the rim shape. For example, the new ENVE SES 6.7 Pro G wheelset is incredibly wide, and fast according to our testing, so it can be more aero with wider tyres. Meanwhile the Hunt Limitless rim is narrower, and has been designed specifically for 40-45mm wide tyres.

Personally, I have used 45mm for events like Graean Gravel, and as a rear tyre for Gralloch. It is a good balance of wide enough for most gravel surfaces, while not being as heavy as a 50mm+.

However, over rough gravel a 50mm tyre does feel more cushioned, and results in less fatigue, while also giving exceptional handling on loose corners. This is a trend that has grown in gravel, with 50-60mm options now being common, and with that, a wider rim is required to really maximise performance.

To that end, the Hunt Limitless 40 rim already shows its age, and the newer 5AM Gravel is a good, more modern alternative, but it does come at a £500 uplift.

The Hunt Limitless 40 gravel wheelset is an impressively good value wheelset. For the difference of 100g and lack of carbon spokes, it is £1000 cheaper than the UD Carbon spoke version with the same rim.

I also appreciate that lockrings, spare spokes, valves and wheel bags have been included, as even on higher range offerings these often get left out, and they are not items I think people should need to consider purchasing when getting a wheelset.

There are other good value offerings available, such as the Parcours FKT (£1249) which is a little heavier, but deeper and designed for wider tyres, and the Reserve 40/44 GR (£1599) and Scope R4.G (£1498) which are both very similar on paper.

Given the inclusion of spares, plus the ease of customer service, certainly in the UK, I am a big fan of the Hunt Limitless 40 wheels.

The only downside to me personally is that the rims could do with being a touch wider for the trend towards 50mm and up in tyres. However, for a lot of gravel riding scenarios, either hardpack or tarmac and bike paths, 45mm is perfectly adequate and these rims are well designed to work with those. If you are planning on tackling looser gravel, large stones, and plenty of wet weather events, then you may find better value in a wider rim to accommodate 50mm+ tyres.

The HUNT Limitless 40 gravel wheelset is such an attractive offering that it makes the higher specification Limitless 40 models with carbon spokes and ceramic bearings appear somewhat obsolete due to the better value of these.

The weight is competitive with more expensive offerings, while performance with 45mm tyres is brilliant.

If you're looking for something a little more performance oriented or futureproof, then the newer 5AM Gravel wheels would be a better bet, but for most people, 45mm tyres can still be the go-to for a lot of gravel riding and racing, and these are a solid choice.

These could look a little more exciting, as matte finishes look dirty quickly, but that is the limit of my critique.

I like a solid rim bed personally, but the tyres seat and hold pressure well, while the hookless performance is good as more tyres adhere to the TSS standard.

I haven’t felt lacking with these wheels at any point, there have been some spoke pings at points but the wheels are in perfect working order.

There are some properly lightweight gravel wheel offerings on the market now at a similar depth, but the HUNT are still very much at the competitive end given the depth and the price.

It’s hard to fault the value here with the price, customer care, and where it sits in the competitive rankings. The only downside I can possibly see is if you want the best aero for 50mm+ tyres, but then those offerings are substantially more expensive

items.title: Tour de France breakaway star heads to Southeast Asia for 2,500km charity solo bike trip – Video
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The 26-year-old Lotto-Intermarché rider is ending his offseason in an alternative way, embarking on a 2,500km, 19-day trip in Vietnam and Cambodia. He's raising funds for Molembike, a charity in Molenbeek, Brussels, which is dedicated to promoting social cohesion through cycling.

Veistroffer will donate €5,000 to the charity, while sponsors Ekoï and Lotto will each contribute €1 for each kilometre he rides during the adventure.

It's a far cry from the usual winter training activities pro racers usually take on in Spain, which Veistroffer described to as "Training camp in Calpe, climbing the Coll de Rates fifty times, doing the same out-and-back route twenty times. The routine for ten years."

He's travelling light on his trip, heading out on an Orbea Terra gravel bike equipped with three panniers and two sets of kit as well as some changes of clothes for the evenings. "I still have room enough to bring back a few souvenirs," he said.

Veistroffer, who turned pro with Lotto last year and won a stage of the Tour of Oman this spring, will document the trip on his YouTube channel. He's uploaded an episode taking viewers through his route planning, schedule, and gear, and on Monday he uploaded the first episode of his travels in Vietnam.

He's set to take on 19 days of riding, each measuring between 140km and 180km, with his only real requirement to make his return flight to Europe on December 2.

"I don't know yet where I'll stop, but I intend to avoid touristy spots," he said.

"The first third of the journey will be fairly flat, through rice paddies. Then, near the Cambodian border, I'll find a mountainous area, passes at 1,500 meters altitude, a more tropical feel; cocoa and coffee fields, magnificent sunsets. Towards the end, I'll follow the South China Sea."

Veistroffer logged 94 race days and 14,248km this season, the most in the professional peloton, but he's showing no signs of slowing down. His Asian trip has the full backing of his Lotto team, of course.

"It's almost a Grand Tour. It's the first of the 2027 season or the last of 2026; it's up to you," he said.

"If it can preserve my mental state and satisfy my need for freedom…"

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘The cardiac Knicks find a way’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The same we thought we’d never see GTA VI hit the proverbial shelves…

Here’s a bunch of quotes and comments coming off another Knicks dub in Toronto.

On Darko Rajaković’s coaching and the Raptors’ defensive intensity:

“Darko does a heckuva job… those guys play hard, really good defensively, give us fits.”

On Jalen Brunson’s late four-point play creating the separation needed to beat Toronto:

“That created the separation that we needed to be able to put them away. So just a big shot. It was one of those things where the play broke down, and we kept looking for an opportunity while spacing the floor. And Jalen found one and let it fly.”

On the Knicks’ late-game execution and contributions from Towns, Anunoby, Bridges and Shamet:

“I thought our execution, especially down the stretch, the last few minutes of the game, was at a pretty high level, on both ends of the floor, but particularly offensively. Our pacing, our spacing, our screening — we took care of the basketball down the stretch.

“We got a lot of different guys that produced in a lot of different ways tonight. Obviously, KAT continues to be a double-double machine. OG [Anunoby] was our defensive player of the game. … Mikal was good for us, especially down the stretch. And Landry Shamet was huge.”

On his improved relationship with Karl-Anthony Towns and the importance of adapting his coaching philosophy:

“It’s just part of being around each other. You hope your relationship with everybody grows. That’s not gonna always happen but you hope it does. KAT’s got a really good feel of how to play the game. Obviously he’s a perennial All-Star. So those things you’ve always got to take into account when it comes to trying to listen or try to adapt more to what their style of play is.

“As a head coach — come in, it’s your first year, and you have an idea what you want to do. Sometimes it doesn’t fit. Offensively, or defensively. And that’s when you’ve got to pivot. And so we kept pivoting and pivoting and building until we found a nice little groove. We feel pretty good about each other right now.”

On recovering from the ankle injury scare after his four-point play:

“Adrenaline was pumping, and went back out there.”

On Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges regaining confidence and contributing to the Knicks’ success:

“This is a huge night for them, the way they played. They’re gaining confidence every single night. They’re going to continue to do great things for us and they’re only going to get better.”

On the Knicks rediscovering their ability to win close games:

“A lot of times when we get in games like that, especially last year, the cardiac Knicks find a way.”

On gaining Mike Brown’s trust and having more input in the team’s strategy:

“It’s more familiarity with the system and building that trust with Mike where he can trust me with things I see and say, which started in the playoffs. So building off that this year. Having more input and him hearing me out.”

On acting as a second coach and collaborating with Brown during games:

“Him trusting me like a second coach. Me and him are always coaching with each other in the game, looking at game plans and plays and maybe ideologies and things I see that can help our team win, especially in close games. Working with him and coaching on the floor. It’s been great. It’s been fun.”

On how his relationship with Brown has improved since the championship run:

“We just grew. We’ve grown with each other. And obviously there’s trust that has to be established and both of us trust each other a lot. And the last playoff run showed it. So just building off that trust and the relationship that was built in the playoffs and having it make our team better this year.”

On Jose Alvarado’s professionalism and importance to the Knicks’ locker room:

“Jose is a consummate professional. He’s probably one of the best locker room guys we have, and one of the best people we have on the bench. His energy, just his presence, with a jersey on or a warmup on, it means more for this team than what the stats show.”

On his recent mental struggles:

“Has been kicking my ass for a couple weeks.”

On stepping up his game on Tuesday after struggling through a few games:

“I think it was a step in the right direction. I think I’m obviously getting into the flow, into the rhythm of things, but today was a step in the right direction. Still a lot to improve on, but you got to start stacking days at some point.”

On how his contract situation can amplify the pressure of poor performances:

“That’s a low-hanging fruit. Sometimes some of those things amplify because you’re in a contract year, essentially. It’s human nature.

“It’s in the back of your mind, and when you start focusing on those things, negative outcomes happen.”

On trying to overcome his struggles and improve his mindset:

“When you’re in the middle of it, there’s not much that can really help. At the end of the day, you just have to go out there. And I think today I had a little bit of a better spirit.”

On the negative thought patterns that have affected his performances:

“I’m struggling to shoot the ball, but it’s one of those things where you start looking at the negatives and that’s all you see. You don’t see some of the positives. Then it’s a snowball effect. One thing happens and you’re trying to get yourself out of a hole that you’re not giving yourself the ability to get out of. It’s about playing with that joyful spirit, looking at things half full instead of half empty.”

On dealing with physical and mental challenges simultaneously:

“For me, this (rough patch) is a little harder because I’m trying to get the mental aspect right and the physical aspect right. It can be easier when you’re just dealing with one of those things. … I’m battling both of those things. I’m trying to give myself a little bit of grace with that.”

On maintaining a positive attitude despite losing his place in the Knicks’ rotation:

“I think it’s more how I was raised [by] my parents. Treat people how you want to be treated. Sometimes the situation isn’t going to be what you want. You can’t control certain things and control what you can and that’s your attitude, your energy every day. So I try to do that.

“I’m human, I have days where it’s not going to be all lovey-dovey. But I always tell myself, ‘Whether I’m not playing or not, I got the best seats in the house.’ And I get to support my teammates. So I try to go with that mindset as best I can and my teammates allow me to be myself.”

On the viral clip showing him comforting Mikal Bridges on the bench:

“[Mikal] is fine. We are all human. The camera caught us that time, but I probably do stuff like that 100 times during a game.”

On staying prepared for opportunities after falling out of the rotation:

“The season is long. I’ve been on the other side. When I first got in the league [in 2021], I wasn’t even touching the court. Then eventually I got to touch the court and get some reps in and played a huge role in the rotation.

“Sometimes you get out of it. The only way to get back is stay ready because an opportunity is going to come, you just don’t know when. So that’s the hardest thing is the guessing game of when that will happen. But you work, work and work and trust that it will come in the end of the day.”

On how close the Raptors came to beating the Knicks in their previous meeting:

“After rewatching and rewatching and rewatching film, we played against the NBA champions and, in my three-and-a-half years here as coach, that’s when we came the closest to beating them. We’re getting better. Just one free throw and the game is completely different.”

items.title: Football Daily | From Cincinnati to Manchester: Pochettino in a hurry to paint town red
items.author: Barry Glendenning
items.content:
With his team mired in the relegation zone and a massive match at Liverpool this weekend, Mauricio Pochettino has been understandably busy since being appointed head coach of Manchester United. Unfortunately for Old Trafford regulars, the small print of his contract meant the Argentinian was tied up masterminding victory for USA USA USA in the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti when he ought to have been in Carrington moving red magnets around a tactics board in front of Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Harry Maguire.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
With his team mired in the relegation zone and a massive match at Liverpool this weekend, Mauricio Pochettino has been understandably busy since being appointed head coach of Manchester United. Unfortunately for Old Trafford regulars, the small print of his contract meant the Argentinian was tied up masterminding victory for USA USA USA in the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti when he ought to have been in Carrington moving red magnets around a tactics board in front of Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Harry Maguire.

The match in Cincinnati was ostensibly a dead rubber, given the hosts kicked off with a 6-0 lead. However, the conditions of Pochettino’s release clause dictated he had to remain in charge until finishing his post-match media duties at the TQL Stadium. Like an errant spouse having one last dinner with their put-upon partner while their lover waits outside the restaurant with the engine running, Pochettino was unable to make his excuses and leave until the bill was settled. It was no surprise that his new role came up during his exit interview. In a playful exchange with DaMarcus Beasley, who spent a season on loan at Manchester City during the (Ben) Thatcher era, something of a gauntlet was thrown down to the departing boss. “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue,” honked the former international, who may be unaware of his former club’s disgrace and potentially imminent relegation to the North West Counties League.

“No way, you will see,” chuckled Pochettino by way of response. “Give me time. Give me time and that is going to change, for sure.” While the future colour scheme of football in Manchester almost certainly lies more in the hands of the three-person independent panel who will decide City’s fate after finding them guilty of industrial scale financial shenanigans, Pochettino assured fans he and his staff will do their bit to ensure the city will be painted red. “We are excited because the new challenge is a big challenge,” he whooped. “But at the same time, it’s the adrenaline that you want to feel. We are going to have a different job, but we have the experience to deal with that. We know that it is not a situation that deserves to be at a club like Manchester United and for the fanbase. The fanbase is amazing.”

Considering they’ve been flirting with Pochettino for nine years, most United fans will be unconcerned by his eventual arrival being delayed by an extra couple of days but, with that game against Liverpool to prepare for, the 54-year-old wasted little time in hightailing it to the airport and boarding a private jet for his new home. Upon arrival, he is expected to oversee his first training session, an event Sky Sports News has melodramatically anticipated using a serene, high-budget cinematic aesthetic that captures our Argentinian hero gazing longingly into a Manchester sunset. It’s a majestic, blockbuster shot that has rightfully become the subject of no end of online mockery. Football Daily wonders if we’ll see a contrasting shot on Sunday, when the Sky cameras cut to Pochettino staring in wide-eyed horror as Liverpool spank yet another goal past his side’s hapless defence.

Join Sarah Rendell at 8pm GMT for updates on Chelsea 2-0 PSG in Women’s Bigger Cup.

“It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done … going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened” – Omar Sowunmi gets his chat on with Will Unwin about his dual life as a top, top model and no-nonsense centre-back with Bromley.

Thanks for drawing my attention to the ‘Pierre Sage playbook for unfussed continental coaches’ ( yesterday’s Football Daily ). Any info about where to order a copy? I’m asking for a newly-employed friend in Manchester” – Mike Wilner.

When I first skimmed over mention of BigShoe (yesterday’s Still Want More? – full email edition), I was shocked to think the likes of Clark’s, Kickers and Bull Boys (signed by him, Alan Hansen ) had formed a global order à la Big Tech, Big Pharma and (possibly) Big Website. Thankfully, it’s a rather life-affirming organisation. Kudos to them and all involved” – Martin Clifford.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com . Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Martin Clifford. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here .
